speechtext: LANCASTER (Lincoln and Nia gara) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No 88) to amend the Railway Act, 1903. He said : The object of the Bill, shortly stated, is to restore the law to what it was up to last session in regard to the filling and packing of frogs, guard-rails and switches on railways for the protection of the men working them. The law up to last year was that the Railway Committee of the Privy Council could dispense with the packing during the months from December to April. Last year, in some way, before the Railway Act was finally passed, the section was amended so as to give the Railway Commission power to dispense with this entirely. The object of this Bill is to provide that the Railway Commission may have power to dispense with the packing during the time provided for in the old law, but not to virtually render the section nugatory. The object, in fact, is to make the law what it was up to last session.

Before the Orders of the Day are called, I wish to draw the attention of the House to the state of the mail service in the Saskatchewan district. I received a telegram to-day from the secretary of the Board of Trade of Rosthern. in my constituency. It is as follows :
Rosthern Board of Trade requests you to urge Postmaster General to hasten transportation of mails, none since fourteenth delays unreasonable for months business men and general public greatly inconvenienced also as to freight situation desperate do what you can.
DR. A. B. STEWART, President Rosthern Board of Trade.
I might say in connection with this matter that I have received by telegram during the past two or three weeks communications of a similar kind from the Boards of Trade of Prince Albert and other places. I can quite understand that owing to the snow blockade of last winter, there might be some reasonable excuse for the company then not being able to deliver the mails. But I am given to understand from the same localities that the company is short of coal, and that that is one of the reasons for the present delay. However I think that at this season of the year the fault rests largely with the company, for the simple reason, that while no mails have gone into or out of that country for fourteen or fifteen days, passengers

have come down and have brought mail with them. If passengers could come down and bring mail matter with them 1 would think that the railway company 'should be forced by the Postmaster General to deliver the mails. I know that the bridge at Saskatoon has been swept away by the flood but there is a ferry on the river and the mails could have been transported on it. The company have quite a number of locomotives between Prince Albert and Saskatoon and also between Saskatoon and Lumsden where I believe the trouble is, as the Qu'Appelle Valley is flooded. But they could get the mail across by boat if they took the trouble. The Canadian Pacific Railway, however, will not take any action and while passengers are able to get through they refuse to take the mail out, and I think they should be forced to do so. I draw the attention of the government to it, and I think the administration should see that the railway carry out their contract, and perform the services for which they are paid.

speechtext: Before this motion is carried I would like to call the attention of the Finance Minister (Mr. W. S. Fielding) to the circulation in this country of the silver of the Straits Settlements. It is exactly similar in its appearance to the Canadian silver coinage and has on one side of it the Queen's head very much like our own coinage. But it is a depreciated coinage. The 50 cent piece I am informed is not worth 20 cents in value and there seems to be an organization, almost a conspiracy-and I am told it is an Oriental conspiracy-to unload great quantities of this silver in Canada. The business men of Toronto, Montreal and other places are complaining of its circulation. It if passed in rapid circulation and every one takes these coins for 50 cent pieces, but when you come to examine it, it is found to be depreciated money of the Straits Settlements. I think it should be the duty of the Canadian government to protest against the use of the Sovereign's head of a depreciated currency, in such a way as to mislead the public and injure tbe silver coinage of colonies whose silver is up to standard. A protest from this government to the home government might be effective. It has been suggested that this 50 cent piece should be made much thicker, or should have some distinctive mark on it such as the square hole which we find in the centre of Chinese coins. In some way our people should be protected from this coinage. I simply wish to ask the Finance Minister (Mr. W. S. Fielding) to consider whether it would not be wise to enter a protest against the circulation of this depreciated silver coinage which so closely resembles the Canadian coinage.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance).
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid we would be hardly justified in entering a protest against the action of another colony which might claim the right to manage its own currency. If there is a dangerous similarity between the coinage of the Straits Settlements and our own, possibly we might have to adopt some alterations in our own coinage. No one is obliged to take silver, which is not a legal tender, and the people have it in their hands to refuse it. But I know that by the practice of commerce the mere fact of its not being tender is not enough ; people take it as they do American coinage. I should be glad to take the matter into consideration, and if the similarity is so dangerous that it requires attention, we may be able to find some solution of the difficulty.	,

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in
reference to this clause which is a clause providing for an extension of time, I desire to oiler a few remarks, and very few they will be. In view of the fact that the right lion. Prime Minister, when he introduced this supplemental agreement practically gave us no reason why the clause contained in the original contract, should be changed so as to grant an extention of time, other than that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company asked for an extension of time, I would earnestly protest against an extension of time as far as it relates, at any rate, to the prairie section. I could understand, that, in view of one year practically having been lost, an extension of time would be asked to cover the mountain section, but I think this clause, if it is designed more particularly to apply to the mountain section,

should specifically say so. It was claimed last year by the Prime Minister that this road was urgently needed to relieve traffic congestion in the west, and that therefore we could not wait for surveys or for information in regard to it. But this year the Prime Minister in introducing the amendment, had only this to say, in connection with section 1, of the amended contract:
The first of these modifications relates to the time within which the line is to he built, and the proposition to which we to-day ask the assent of parliament is in these terms :
Sec. 1.-Notwithstanding anything in the said contract contained, the time for completion of the western division of the railway shall be and the same is hereby extended to the first day of December, 1911, and the tenth paragraph of the said contract is amended accordingly, and by inserting the word ' strikes ' after the word ' floods ' in the seventh line thereof.
By the terms of section 10 of the contract submitted to parliament last session, it is provided that the western section of the line, the portion from Winnipeg to the Pacific ocean, should he built within the period of five years commencing December 10, 1903. The company thought that this limit of time was perhaps a little too short and the only modification which they asked was that in case of failure on their part to comply with this condition of the contract, the deposit of $5,000,000 should not be forfeited. Their application- was in these terms :
Time for the completion of the construction of the western division, fixed as December 1, 1908, is considered short. Failure to complete within the time should at least not create a forfeiture of the deposit.
We did not altogether agree to this, but we provided that the time should be extended by three years so that the company will have until December 1, 1911, in which to complete their line.
These are all of the concessions which have been made except that to the legitimate causes for delay, such as floods, disturbances, &e., strikes are added. I am sure that our hon. friends on the other side of the House will have no objection to agree to this modification of the contract.
The only reason that the Prime Minister assigned for tlie extension of time was, that the company thought that three years was too short. The company did not offer any very strenuous objection to the five year limit, but the Prime Minister thought it well to grant the extension for three years longer, and so he dissipated all his arguments of last year in favour of immediate construction. I, as a western member, am most anxious to see the road constructed to meet the wants and requirements of our people at the earliest possible date ; I protest against this extension of time so far as it relates to the 1,000 miles of the prairie section. There is no reason why the road should not be constructed on the prairie within the time fixed in last year's Bill. The Canadian Pacific Railway did not take five years to construct its line on the prairie, at a time when the facilities for quick railway construction were not nearly so modern 70
as they are now. It may be, that the mountain section would require a longer time to build, but the prairie section through the grain-growing country, can be very well completed by the 1st of December, 1908.
1 wish also to ask the Minister of Justice, if the government can give any information, relatively speaking, as to where this road is going to be constructed west of Winnipeg. The company have had survey parties out during the past year, and we would like to know if reports have been made indicating where the road is going to run ; or is it the intention of the government to leave this an open question until after the general election. Recently the Liberal candidates in Manitoba have been going around with maps pretending to show the proposed location of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and of course as each member points it out as running through his own constituency, the thing is reduced to an absurdity, but nevertheless it is held out as a bribe practically to the electors. Indeed, one of the leading Liberal papers in the west has declared that the electors have it in their power to say where this road is to be constructed, and their opinions on the matter would be largely judged by the result of the elections. That is very candid, but at the same time it is very unjust, very unfair, and very misleading. I protest against the location of this line being postponed until after the general elections, and I hold that this Bill should not pass until the government declares what will be the location of the line west of Winnipeg. Surely they can at least tell us whether it is going to run north or south of the Canadian Northern. Last year when the member for North Simcoe (Mr. MacCarthy) who had charge of the Bill, was asked whether the line would run north or south of the Canadian Northern, he said he was not sure, but he thought it was north : and when we pointed out that the map circulated by the Grand Trunk Railway "located the line to the south, he candidly admitted that until the surveys were made that could not be ascertained. If the government desires to have the time extended for the completion of the mountain section, let them say so, but there is no reason on earth why that line cannot be constructed within five years through the prairie country, where relief is needed at the earliest possible moment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman will realize that it will be to the interest of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company to have that section of the line constructed at the earliest possible moment, because it has always been described in this House as being the fat section, or the revenue-producing section, so far as local traffic is concerned. Under the original agreement, it is provided that the western section is to be finished within five years from the last of December. 1903, and it is also provided that a sum of $5,000,000 is to be deposited, which will be



219G
forfeited In case the road is not completed from Winnipeg to the Pacific ocean, and equipped with respect to the whole road. The gentlemen who have put up that deposit are naturally somewhat anxious that no forfeit should take place in the event of non-compliance with the strict terms of the agreement, and the suggestion was made, that we should declare that the deposit would not be forfeited in the event of the non-completion of the road within that time. We thought it infinitely preferable in the interest of the country, that instead of releasing the deposit we would extend the delay, and instead of declaring that the $5,000,000 should not be forfeited if the road were not constructed, we should declare the $5,000,000 should not be forfeited, if the road were completed within eight years. My hon. friend (Mr. W. J. Roche) has referred to the rapid construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and I would ask him to bear in mind, that as it was the interest of the Canadian Pacific Railway to construct their road as rapidly as possible, it will be the interest of the Grand Trunk Pacific to complete this part of the line at the earliest possible moment.
My hon. friend will remember that the Canadian Pacific had authority to extend the construction of its line over a period of ten years. As a matter of fact, the first sod on the main line was turned on the 2nd of May, 1881, the last spike was driven on the 7th of November, 1885, and the first eastbound through train arrived at Montreal on the 12th July, 1886, or a little more than five years after the road was first begun ; and I am quite sure that with the facilities for railway building that now exist in the Northwest, this road can be completed within the same length of time. At the same time, it seems to me that it is not unreasonable to expect that the gentlemen who are depositing their $5,000,000 will see to it that such precautions are taken on their part, that that deposit will not be forfeited by the country in consequence of the non-fulfilment of the contract in that respect -that is, if they do not completely construct the road and completely equip it, not partly, but ready for operation within the time specified. Under these circumstances, I think my hon. friend will see that this is a very reasonable request. The location of the line has to proceed in the same way and under the same conditions as any other private railway built by a private company. The company will, in their own interest, endeavour to locate it in such a way as to derive the greatest possible amount of revenue from the local traffic. On the other hand, the government will have something to say with respect to the location ; and it will be the duty of the government to consider the location from the standpoint of the general interest of the country at large as well as from the standpoint of the local interest concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext: Will the Minister of Justice read that portion of the Bill which says that the government will have the approval of the location of the road in the province of Manitoba. I think it refers to the Northwest Territories.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Section 122' of the General Railway Act applies to this road as well as to any other private enterprise, and not a mile of it can be constructed without the plans of the location being deposited with the Minister of Railways and being approved by him acting for the government. So that this road in its entirety must be controlled by the government. Therefore, it will be in the interest of the company to locate the road so that it will be of the greatest advantage to the country and develop the greatest local traffic. It will also be the duty of the government to see .that the location of the line is such as will not only be advantageous for local traffic but in the interest of the country at large. It will be our duty to see that these two interests are harmonized; and 1 am quite sure that in the location of the line, the only two interests concerned-that of the company with respect to the revenue-producing power of the road, and that of the government with respect to the interests of the country at large-the interest of the people of Manitoba and the Northwest will receive a large share of consideration. It is impossible to say at present just where the road will be located. The measure of last session was not through parliament until the close of the working season, and very little has been done this season. So far as my knowledge goes, no report has yet been made by the company with respect to their intentions as to the location of the line.

The hon. minister has stated one thing in which I do not concur ; that is, that it would be in the interest of the company to have the road constructed at the earliest possible moment. In view of the fact that Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson has stated that the liability of the company does not begin until after the road has been completed, I think it will be to their advantage to delay construction to the last moment, so long as they get it completed within the eight years. The Minister of Justice refers to the completion of the line as a whole ; but I am dwelling on the most important part of it, the prairie section. I am not objecting so much to a certain extension of time for the construction of the mountain section ; but I am directing my objection to the extension of time so far as it relates to the 1,000 miles of easy construction across the prairie, that part of the country which requires relief at the earliest possible moment; and in view of the fact that the liability of the Grand Trunk Company under their guarantee does not begin until after the road is completed, I do not know that

they will be anxious to have it constructed very quickly.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I cannot agree with my hon. friend as to the company not being liable until the road is completed. I think it is the liability of the government that does not begin until after the road is completed, not the liability of the Grand Trunk Pacific.
I am not concerned as to the construction put upon this agreement by Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson; I am concerned about the construction that the words bear and that we are going to put upon them ourselves. It is perfectly immaterial to me how Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson may have interpreted the agreement at a meeting of his shareholders ; what is important is how we are going to interpret it. Now, I do not want to separate the two parts of the western division more than is necessary ; I want to treat them as a unit. With respect to the forfeit, we will deal with the revenue-producing centre as well as with that portion of the road which has been considered to be the lean section. I want the section from Winnipeg to the Pacific coast to be considered as a unit, and any departure from that I will endeavour to prevent. Undoubtedly it is to the interest of Manitoba and the Northwest that the prairie section should be completed at the earliest possible moment. Undoubtedly that is in the interest of the company also. But it is in the interest of the people at large that the road shall be constructed from the Pacific coast to Winnipeg at the earliest possible moment, and that is what we want. We do not want to distinguish between the two portions. We do not want to give the impression that we consider one section of immediate and vital importance and the other section as being of remote importance. We want the whole railway constructed as rapidly as possible ; and we hope that by giving this reasonable extension, the company will realize that it is the wish of the people of Canada that the road shall be constructed in its entirety from the! Pacific to Winnipeg at the earliest possible moment.
Passing from the completion of the* road for a moment, can the minister tell the House and the public when the commencement of the road is likely to take place ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The intention is, and this contract provides, that the construction shall be begun immediately.

What does the minister mean by immediately ? Has he not some progress to report, or some information to give as to what steps the Grand Trunk Pacific Company are now taking to start work immediately ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have not any information beyond the casual information that has come to me to the effect that surveying parties have been out and have ex-701
amined the country from Winnipeg westward and from Winnipeg eastward for a certain distance. That is a general sort of information which my hon. friend has as well as I, but on which I cannot ask the House to rely. The position, I take it, is this, in so far as the company is concerned. Until such time as they have a binding contract-a contract binding upon the country as it is upon the company-we cannot expect them to enter into any very large works of construction.
Will this contract be binding on the company once it has passed this House ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If my hon. friend will read the agreement, he will see that we insist that the contract shall be ratified, in the first instance, by the shareholders of the Grand Trunk Railway before we submit it to the House at all ; and having obtained the consent of the Grand Trunk Pacific and the ratification of the Grand Trunk Railway, then we ask the approval of the House.

I cannot see that the hon. minister has given any good reason for extending the time for constructing that portion of the road to which my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. W. J. Roche) has referred. We all know that the Canadian Pacific Railway built its line over the prairies at the rate of one mile per day. If it be in the interests of the people, as lion, gentlemen opposite urge, that the whole of this road should be completed as soon as possible, then this portion, which is to be the fat portion and the portion which they say furnishes the main reason for building this road at all, ought to be pushed through without delay, and I can see no reason why the government should extend the time for building it. Certainly the hon. minister has not given any good reason why the company has been given an extension of time. There is no doubt t(mt there are portions of that western country to which this proposed road will give relief. I have been shown maps indicating two or three different directions in which supporters of the government say this line is to go, starting from Winnipeg, and no doubt if it be built through some of these places it will do a great deal of good. I therefore cannot see why the government should give the company three years longer in which to build that line, especially when it might be built across the whole of the prairie in two years or possibly three years at the outside. While this proposition is not one that I am in favour of-and I made that very clear last session when I moved a resolution for the extension of a government railway across this continent, which resolution the whole Conservative party supported and the en-

tire Liberal party opposed

while that is the ease, I can see no reason why the government should extend the length of time as it is doing.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Does my hon. friend wit realize that the selfish interests of fli*' company will prompt it to construct /this road across the prairies within the /shortest possible time ? My hon. friend I from Marquette referred to the liability I of the government. As I read this contract, | the liability of the government to endorse 1 the bonds of the company begins only after 1 the road is completed-after it is built I from the Pacific ocean to Winnipeg and S equipped in its entirety. The interest of | the company-if we have succeeded in identifying the Grand Trunk Railway with the Grand Trunk Pacific, as we think we have-is to complete that road at the earliest possible moment, because in the interval, except in so far as the government may be pleased to come to their assistance, they are obliged to finance the whole enterprise. In their own interest, therefore, they will construct this portion Cj the road at the earliest possible moment.
If it be both in the interests of the company and of the people to have that road speedily constructed, why not make the limit of time four years ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Because that is not necessary.

The hon. gentleman is relying on the selfish interests of the company, which he says will compel them to build this road with the shortest possible delay. If that be the case, why not put it in the contract ?
Mr, FITZPATRICK. I am depending upon something that in my experience has never failed-the selfish interests of public corporations.
That is a new doctrine for the Liberal party.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
If my hon. friend the Minister of Justice is depending solely on that consideration, he might strike out some other portions of the contract, for example, the clause with reference to the operation. Yet that has not been eliminated. I am inclined to think that the promoters) of this scheme did not press very strongly for any such extension of time as is to be found here. At least I should judge so from the correspondence. As my hon. friend from Marquette has said, the only suggestion which came from the promoters is this :
Time for the completion of the construction of the western division, fixed as December 1st, 190S, is considered short. Failure to complete within the time should at least not create a forfeiture of the deposit.

You will observe that they do not put it very strongly, rather very mildly. Then it must not be forgotten that they have very ample safeguards against any difficulties which may ar'ise during the progress of construction :	For example,
by clause 10 of the agreement, it is provided as follows :
The work of locating and constructing the said western division shall be commenced forthwith after the ratification of -this agreement by the parliament of Canada and shall proceed with the utmost despatch and shall be completed within five years from the 1st day of December, 1903, unless prevented by the act of God, the King's enemies, internal disturbances, epidemics, floods or other causes beyond the control of the company.
To those causes have now been added, by this proposed enactment, the word ' strikes,' so that the company is safeguarded in every respect against any possible cause which might arise and prevent completion of the road within the time limited. My hon. friend says that the Canadian Pacific Railway, although a much longer period was given for its completion, was completed in four years from the time of its commencement ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In five years.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I thought it was from 1881 to 1885.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If we take the turning of the first sod and the driving of the last spike, the road was open for operation within five years.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I will accept my hon. friend's correction. It was opened within five years. And, at this day, conditions for the building of railways are improved. There are better opportunities in the Northwest, I imagine, to build a railway now than there were then-greater facilities at hand. Then, within the last quarter of a century, I fancy, the progress in the art of railway building has been very considerable. Now, if the Canadian Pacific Railway could be completed in about four years and opened for traffic in less than five years, why is so long a period allowed for the completion of this line ? Important considerations arise. The first is, what time will you fix for the completion of the line from Winnipeg to the coast ? And the second is, if you are to extend the time, would it not have been practicable and would it not have been better so far as some portions of the line are concerned, to require they should be completed within much shorter time? I realize that the proposal of the government-and I am looking at it from their standpoint-is a proposal for a line from ocean to ocean. But, even looking at it from that standpoint, we must not shut our eyes to the fact that the traffic to which the company looks, the

larger portion of that traffic arising in the west, for a good many years will probably be eastward bound. Therefore, it seems to me there is, as pointed out by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. W. J. Roche) possibly more urgency in respect of the prairie division than the mountain division. I am not minimizing for a moment the importance of the mountain division, but we have to recognize the conditions and if the mountain division is more difficult, we must necessarily allow more time for its completion. Under the circumstances, it would seem to me to have been a very proper thing on the part of the government, in proposing an amendment to this clause, to have had regard to the importance of its eastern connection. So far as the eastern division of the road is concerned, the date of its completion is entirely within the power of the government. It can complete it as rapidly as the resources of the country will permit. Then, to connect with the eastern division, you have what is called the prairie section of the western division. The company is allowed, under the terms of the contract, a period of eight years within which to complete the line from Winnipeg to Edmonton. Now, how far is that a reasonable allowance ? Has my hon. friend the Minister of Justice any information as to what would be a reasonable time to allow in respect of the prairie section ? It seems to me that in considering the proposed extension of the time, and especially having regard to the qualifications that are imposed by section 10 of the original contract upon the liability of the company,, the government in making this proposed amendment ought to afford the House some expert information as to what would be a reasonable distance per year for the company to build, it has been suggested to me by gentlemen who profess to be familiar with these matters-who certainly have more experience than I have-that a period of three years would be ample time for the construction of the road from Winnipeg to Edmonton, unless the company were impeded by some of the causes which are excepted under section 10 of the original contract. Well, these exceptions do not stand in the way, because section 10 expressly provides that, where the company is delayed, by any of these causes over which they have no control, the delay so caused shall not be counted against them. Therefore they have eight years, under the provisions of this contract, eight years of good working time in which they can proceed with the construction not only of the line to the Pacific coast, but of the line from Winnipeg to Edmonton. I would again suggest to my hon. friend the Minister of Justice that some expert opinion ought to be furnished to the House before this committee is required to pass upon
so important a portion of the contract as this. I do not wish to go over matters of ancient history ; but it would not be out of place, perhaps, for me to remind not only the Minister of Justice, but the Prime Minister that we had very strong language from the Prime Minister on this question last year. I will not quote at any length from my right hon. friend's (Sir Wilfrid Laurier's) speech, because he does not like me to indulge in too lengthy quotations. But just a few lines may better illustrate what I mean. He said :
Now, Sir, we lay it down as a principle, upon which we are to he judged by friend and foe, that we are to have a transcontinental railway, that its terminus must be in Canadian waters, and that the whole line, every inch of it, must be in Canadian territory. We say further that such a line is a necessity of our commercial independence.
And further on :
What are your minds running to when you have facts staring you in the face which show you that at this moment Canada is not commercially independent of the United States ?
And further on :
But my hon. fpiends opposite are aware that this privilege

referring to the bonding privilege :


has always been held over our heads by the
American authorities as a sword of Damocles.
Now, if there is a sword of Damocles hanging over our heads, and if we can get rid of it within a period of four years, as, we can according to the Minister of Justice, why should we trust merely to the interest of the company, and why should we not impose upon them a stipulation which is to be regarded as a fair stipulation according to that statement ? This was regarded as a matter of great urgency last year, not only so far as the western division was concerned, but so far as the entire line was concerned-and I shall refer to the eastern division a little later on. Instead of the very great urgency which confronted us last year, instead of the very great haste which we are told at that time was necessary, we have the government coming down with an amendment, apparently not very strenuously insisted upon by the gentlemen who are promoting this line, which adds three years to the period fixed for the completion of this road. Now, if the position taken by the Prime Minister last year was a correct position- and upon that position he staked his policy and this measure-then, I venture to submit that there has been no justification shown for the extension provided for by this amendment. Further, let me say to my hon. friend the Minister of Justice that, when he spoke in response to my hon. friend from East York (Mr. Maclean) with regard to the commencement

of the construction of this railway, he perhaps did not bear in mind that it was the duty of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company to begin the work of locating and constructing immediately after the Act of last session had passed. There can be no doubt about that. The agreement of last year was ratified by parliament on the 21th of October and the 25th of October was the day for commencing the work of locating and constructing the said western division should have commenced. So, the inquiry of my hon. friend from East York is an entirely pertinent and just one, and one which should have a more definite and pertinent answer than the Minister of Justice has given.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: Why either ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Because, although the country has made some progress since 1880, and has advanced since that time, there is to-day an element of difficulty in the construction of railways that did not exist in 1880, the difficulty of obtaining labour. It is more difficult to-day to get labour than it was in 1880, although there was no road to the prairie in 1880 and although there is to-day a road extending from Montreal to St. John, N.B., to the Pacific ocean, every one knows that it would be more difficult for the Grand Trunk Pacific to get labour in that country to do that work than it was for the Canadian Pacific in 1880. For example, the Canadian Paci-Ific in' 1880, could get Oriental (labour, there was no objection to Oriental labour in 1880 ; to-day there is a prohibitory tax against Oriental labour. Mongolians cannot come in to work without payment of the tax of $500, but in 1880, they could be imported free and for this reason alone the Grand Trunk Pacific will be at a disadvantage as compared with the Canadian Pacific. Apart from the question of Mongolian labour, if we speak only of the question of white labour, every one knows that to-day one of the difficulties of all kinds of industry, is to get labour, and the Grand Trunk, as prudent men, have to see to it that the difficulties they might find in their way owing to the very prosperity of the country, jwere guarded 'against and for this reason they took some latitude in order not to jeopardize the $5,000,000 they put in our hands, as an earnest that they would go on with the work as speedily as possible. However, if I rightly apprehend the motive which has prompted the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. W. J. Roche) and the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Boyd) to put as strongly as they did the question of time, it is the desire to hace an immediate location of the road. They have not put this forward but it is evidently in the back of their minds. The amendment which has been made does not affect by one iota the immediate location of the line. My friends point to the map and ask whether the railway is to pass here or there. I suppose that every one west of Lake Superior, wants to have this line at his own door. We find that when a railroad is to be built every one wants it as near to his own premises as possible. This condition will exist until the line is located,

but the extension of the time will not affect that question at all.

The statement made by the Minister of Justice and also used by the Prime Minister throws a lot of light upon the situation. They speak of the selfish interests being the impelling motive with the company, and every company. Perhaps the selfish interest of the company suggested that this agreement and this new agreement is simply catering to the selfish interest of the concern. That admission may also go a long way to explain the non-performance of certain things by companies of that kind, notably the Grand Trunk, that company is on record to-day as having given a solemn undertaking to give the people between Montreal and Toronto a penny-a-mile rate. I asked the Minister of Justice about this last year and he did not say it was not the law. He gave evasive answers. I believe that according to bis own words, selfish interests is the impelling reason why that law is not carried out. It is a good confession to have here to-day, that selfish interest is lie impelling motive of corporations.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Is the world a corporation ?	.

The world is a corporation, but I do not define corporations in the way both of the hon. gentlemen have done. As to this question of labour, should not some steps be taken to attract white labour to this country if we have not that labour ? The question is a serious one, there is a cry for labour in this country, and I would ask if the government have any policy or any proposal to suggest to the country whereby this labour difficulty may be overcome? It is true that legislation has been passed which prevents Chinese labour coming in-I do not think it applies to the Japs.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It applies to the Japs in so far as the Japanese restrict their own emigration.

But I do not think our law would prevent them ?
Sir WILFRID LAURIER, Oh, no, but my hon. friend knows that the Japanese government does restrict its own emigration.

But they may withdraw their restriction any day and the country may be- flooded with Japanese labour just as the Japs have covered this country with the depreciated silver to which I referred a minute ago. The Prime Minister has confessed that there is a scarcity of labour ; what does the government propose to do to supply labour to build the road at an early date ? We know that the Canadian Pacific Railway contractors built the road in half the time specified, and I have no
doubt that this road can be built at the rate r.ot of one mile, but of five miles a day, without costing the company anything more. This would relieve the congested state of traffic that they say now characterizes the Northwest. This road can be constructed in a much shorter time than in 1880 as railway construction has now been brought down to a fine art. There are any number of improved contrivances for building railways and the government, especially in view of the statement that time could not wait, should insist upon having the contract of such a character that the road would be completed in a very short time. It can be completed much more quickly than the Canadian Pacific Railway was completed, and if that is the case, why should it not be put in this contract ?

I cannot understand the reasoning of the right hon. gentleman when he says the Canadian Pacific Railway were given ten years to construct their line of railway, and that the first train was run over the road on the 12th of July, 1886, six years after the commencement of the road.
We all know perfectly well that in the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway through that country in those days they had no facilities for bringing in rails, ties and other materials necessary in connection with the construction of the road. The difference between then and now is very great because we have two lines of railway that can assist in bringing in material for the purpose of the construction of this railway. Then, there is the question as to labour. Admitting the hon. gentleman's argument that labour is scarce, see the difference in the amount of labour it would require to bring the material into the country in the days of the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway and now. The material would be brought in over the lines of railway already constructed. The result will be that owing to the changed conditions, the same amount of labour for the transportation of materials will not be required now as was required in the days of the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway. Then, as to the class of labour to be employed on the railway, will -the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company employ what we call natural white labour '-not at all. They are employing to-day very largely Polacks, and Chinamen who are engaged in railway construction year in and year out. They do this work as a matter of choice. These men are railway labourers and do practically nothing else year in and year out and railway contractors prefer that class of labour. They send to the United States and import that class of labour into this country notwithstanding the fact that we have an alien labour law.	.
I was a little mystified as to the discussion that took place in regard to the location of

this line in the west. I merely drew the attention of the hon. Minister of Justice to the fact that certain persons in the west are claiming that this line of railway is going to run through such and such a district. The hon. Minister of Justice replied to that by referring us to section 122 of the general railway Act which contains provisions in regard to ' map,' ' application for approval of map,' 'application of proceedings,' 'plan, profile and book of reference ' and so on, meaning that the location of the line will have to be submitted for approval before it can be determined upon. That would therefore go to prove that statements made by any persons at this date that this line of railway is going to run through any particular section of the west are entirely unwarranted and must simply be regarded as being manufactured out of whole cloth. The right hon. leader of the government says that every man wants to have the railway run through his district. That may be true but every man cannot have the railway through his district. There can only be one line of railway wherever it may be located. Certainly it has not been located, and I am glad that it has been made plain that any person claiming that this line of railway will run through any particular dishict is not justified in making such a claim.

I think the hon. Minister of Justice might well inform the House on one point and that is whether or not, when this application was made to extend the time for the completion of the western division, the government made any attempt to secure the earlier construction of the prairie section than will result from this extension of time. When we find that practical men of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, the president, the general manager and almost all the directors of the company were prepared to sign a contract pledging themselves to build the road in a shorter time, and when, in order to allay the apprehensions of their shareholders they asked for an extension of time, surelv it would have been a proper thing for the government to have endeavoured to have secured the completion of the prairie section at as early a date as possible.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not think there would have been any difficulty in inducing the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company to consent to an earlier construction of the prairie section, but we felt that the object of the people was to secure the construction of a through line from Winnipeg to the coast. We felt, in regard to the construction of the prairie section, that there would be no difficulty whatever, that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company would take care of that. They will get into the fat section, into the wheat lands of the Northwest Territories and they will take care to have their arrangements made in such a Mr. INGRAM.
way that they will get their fair share of the abundant traffic which that country will afford. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition referred a moment ago to the exemptions that were contained in clause 10. These exemptions are the usual exemptions to be found in ordinary contracts. I cannot say, speaking from memory, that the words used here are the words used in all contracts, but they are the words generally used in contracts made with the Public Works Department or the Department of Railway and Canals. I think they are the usual words to be found in these contracts.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I think so.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As to the expert opinion as to the time in which this road can be constructed, of course, the suggestion made by* my hon. friend is the natural suggestion that comes to a man who considers matters of this sort. I must confess that at the time these modifications were being considered, I discussed the question with those acting for the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. I had in my mind that there would be no difficulty in inducing them to agree to the construction of a large part of this railway extending as far as Edmonton within a reasonable short delay, but when I endeavoured to fasten them down to the exact delay within which they would be prepared to do it, and when I pointed out what had been accomplished by the Canadian Pacific Railway the answer they made to me was : We have to take into consideration clause 11 of the contract which read as follows :
The company shall lay out, construct and equip the said western division of the said railway to a standard not inferior to the main line of the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada between Montreal and Toronto

That is not the standard which the Canadian Pacific built up to

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I do not know that the Prime Minister has any justification for regarding me as a convert. I am entitled for the purpose of my argument to view this contract from the standpoint in which it was regarded by the majority of the House last year, and so I shall regard it. The view of the right hon. gentleman last year was, that there was a tremendous crisis in the country; that the sword of Damocles was hanging over our heads, and that we could not afford to say :	wait, wait, or to consider
to-morrow. We were told by my right hon. friend that it was a time for action, but having last year announced these patriotic sentiments, this year he extends for three years, the time during which the sword of Damocles is to hang over us. The Minister cf Justice says that the Grand Trunk managers and shareholders would be fakirs If they did not carefully consider all their responsibility, but what about the gentlemen who signed their names to this contract last year ? Didn't they know all about the question of labour then, and was there any change in labour conditions between the month of October, 1903, and the month of February, 1904 ? I am aware of none. There was the same restriction on Oriental

labour in both months, but nevertheless in the interval, we have the time for the completion of this line extended for three jears. The Minister of Justice says to-day, that it was the duty of the Grand Trunk Company to carefully consider all this, but last year we were told again and again bj the ministers of the Crown, that the men who had Signed the contract, were the ablest railway men in the world, that they had carefully considered and carefully weighed every difficulty that could be presented. I have here quotations from the speeches of the ministers avowing in the strongest possible language to the House and to the country, that every line and every sellable of that contract had been weighed and considered by the ablest railway men of the country, and that they agreed with the government in the interpretation of the contract, and had decided that these stipulations were reasonable and easily carried out. But to-day, we have an amendment offered to the House, and offered without any satisfactory statement of the reasons which lead the government to consent to it. Viewing it from the standpoint of what the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice have said, it does not seem to me that there is any justification for the government taking this course.

Probably these modifications have been made because of. the conditions of the money market in England as well as the condition of the labour market here. In view of the recent experience of the Minister of Finance in the English money market, has he any information to give us as to whether the existing financial condition has had anything to do with the extension of time for the completion of the contract ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: One of the amendments relates to financial matters, and the reason for it having been fully discussed in the House. Certainly, the question of finance had something to do with it.
Is it not a fact that considerable assistance was given by this parliament ?
No, not for hundreds of miles of the Canadian Northern within the boundaries of the province. That was the only guarantee, and it practically paid for the road.
What parts of the line ?

The Rossburn extension in my own constituency, the Carman extension, and a number of other lines. By the way, the other day the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. McCreary) interrupted me to state that the original cost of the Canadian Northern was $20,000 a mile. I would not wish a better argument. That line had been built and in operation for ten years ; it was fully equipped ; towns had been built along the line ; it was a splendid going concern ; and yet the whole business was secured by the provincial government for $20,000 a mile. I would not wish a better argument than that comparison to show that the estimated cost of the prairie section of this road is excessive. Then, corporations can juggle with their accounts in such a way as to make the government's guarantee to the extent of $13,000 a mile cover almost the total cost. The Prime Minister who was so very anxious last year for the' completion of this road that he could not wait, appears now to be the obstructive power, for he is throwing difficulties in the way to show why it would not be fair to expect the company to construct the road within the original time limit of five years. Any of the arguments used to-day would have been equally strong applied to the Bill as it passed the House last session. Since the road is going to be constructed, we are anxious to see it constructed at the earliest possible moment, and not used, as it is being used in my constituency, as a political factor, not only by the gentleman who is contesting Marquette in the Liberal interest, but by the gentleman who is contesting the constituency north of that as well.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Let me make my meaning clear in what I said about Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson. The position I take is that this contract is to be construed according to the terms used in the contract itself, and not according to the construction which Sir- Charles Rivers-Wilson puts upon it or the construction which we may put upon it. Neither of us by the terms we use make the rule of construction to be applied. The contract itself is the law of the parties. If Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson used the language which my hon. friend puts in his mouth with respect to the obligations of the Grand Trunk Railway as distinct from the Grand Trunk Pacific, he is right to this extent, that neither of the Grand Trunk Railway nor the government is under any legal obligation to incur any liability whatever with respect to this road, until such time as it is completed, but in the interval the money for its construction must be found somewhere. The Grand Trunk Pacific may provide it with the help of the Grand Trunk Railway or out of its own resources, but there is no obligation on the government to do anything. If the Grand Trunk Pacific has put up $5,000,000, which will be forfeited should the road not be completed within the time fixed, have we not an assurance that the road will be built at the earliest possible moment ? Is the Grand Trunk Pacific going to run the risk of having that deposit forfeited ? Will that company allow that money to remain unused all this time and pay interest on it and not proceed as rapidly as possible with the construction of the road ?	.
They lose nothing. They pay no interest on the $5,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend is much stronger in financial matters than I am. I have only the experience of an advised financier, and not of one who has to do financing himself. But I can say that any man who goes to a bank and borrows $5,000,000 must pay something to get it, and I happen to know what is paid in this matter. These gentlemen did not get it for nothing.

The hon. gentleman need not be quite so sarcastic. He is a good lawyer, but has not lost his common sense by reason of that fact. He knows perfectly well that there is an undertaking on the part of the government to pay interest on that deposit. True, there is an understanding that there is no interest to be paid by the government in the meantime, because the deposit in the bank is simply on call and may be used by the bank, but there may be also a very good understanding with the Grand Trunk Railway that that company *shall not pay any interest.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The government pay no interest to the Grand Trunk Railway, and the government get no interest on its deposit, but how about the bank ? Who is paying the bank ? Not the government. My hon. friend some time ago said that the estimate for the cost of construction is rather high. My information is that $20,000 a mile is not an exaggerated estimate for a road of this standard.
For the prairie section ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, for the prairie section. This is not to be a road consisting simply of rails put on ties across the prairie, but a road of a standard equal to that of the Grand Trunk Railway between Montreal and Toronto.

What I would like to point out is that if you were to spend $100,000 a mile on this road across the prairie section, you could not make it equal to the Grand Trunk Railway between Toronto and Montreal. That would require time. Year after year the Grand Trunk Railway is ballasted, and that is what makes the quality of that road between Montreal and Toronto.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have, of course, to defer in this matter to the judgment of my hon. friend, but I take it for granted that the Grand Trunk Railway authorities knew what they were doing when they entered into this contract. Perhaps they were entirely in error, but I was under the impression that when they spoke of a road of a certain standard, that meant a road with so many ties per mile, rails of a certain weight-, embankments of a certain quality, and also ballasting of a certain quality. If you consider the question of embankments, ties, rails and ballasting, you have all you need take into account, apart from the grades and curvatures, in order to fix the standard of a railway. Unless prevented by the act of God, the King's enemies, internal disturbances, floods, strikes, or other causes beyond the control of the company.

upon him the simultaneous commencement of the eastern section-that was before the government undertook to! build this section themselves-and even as to that, Mr. Hays promised that as soon as the surveys would be completed, he would push the work on the eastern section simultaneously with the other sections. Therefore, Mr. Hays had an opportunity of considering, even before he signed the first contract, whether he would undertake this construction within the time specified. I would point out that this contract reads very differently from any other contract made by the government. There is an unwritten understanding that if a contractor does everything that it is possible for him to do, he may depend upon the fair play and equity of the other contracting party, to look for necessary modifications. I'n this particular instance the equity of the case has not been taken into consideration by the contracting parties. Every argument advanced by the Prime Minister for the construction of this road, has been based on the ground of urgency, and it is not fair to that western country which awaits development, nor is it fair to the argument of the Prime Minister himself, that the time for the completion of this railway should be extended to eight years. I have visited the prairie section of the country, and I know that there is urgent demand for railway facilities. We recognized that last year when, in the hope of affording immediate relief, we granted extraordinary aid to the Canadian Northern Railway. I regret to say that that company has not done as much work during the last year as we had hoped they would do. We have settlers away up above Battleford and in the Barr colony, and further in the interior, who are anxiously expecting the advent of a railway, If we are going to give these corporations all the latitude they ask for, we cannot expect much equity from them ; we can only expect to get the cold letter of their contract. It may be in the interest of the Grand Trunk Pacific to build that road rapidly, but nevertheless, the report of the meeting of the Grand Trunk shareholders shows, that they banked more or less on the .fact that, they will have eight years instead of fivei years in which to complete construction. If it be the case, as we were told Inst year, that we cannot alter a word or a line in this contract, it may be idle talk for us on this side of the House to point out the duty of that government, but be that as it may, it is incumbent upon us to emphasize the stipulations which should be introduced into that contract in the interests of the people of Canada. In all probability, eight years is not too long to allow for the completion of the mountain section, but it is undoubtedly a fact, that they should complete the prairie section within a shorter delay. The Canadian Northern Railway Company have got to the great lakes, and

I hope that the government will consent to have the agreement restored to what it was as regards the time for building the prairie section. I do not see any reason why the Grand Trunk Railway should object. We are told that it will be in their interest to complete the road as soon as possible. That may or may not be the case, but if so, why not put it in the agreement ?

I have listened with a great deal of attention to the question put by the hon. member for Marquette and the replies given by the Minister of Justice and the First Minister. As I understood the question put by my hon. friend from Marquette, it was this : Why has the time for the construction of the prairie section been extended to eight years ? And I have not heard from either the Minister of Justice or the First Minister any reply to that question, unless the statement made by the Minister of Justice may be considered a reply. But knowing that hon. gentleman as I do, I can hardly conceive that he made that statement seriously. The reason I understood him to give as that which induced the government to extend the time for the construction of the prairie section was its anxiety that there should be harmony in the provisions of this agreement. He was so anxious about the harmonious arrangement of the contract that he would not allow any difference to be made between the time limit for the construction of the prairie section and the mountain section. I can hardly doubt that the hon. gentleman laughed in his sleeve when advancing that as a serious answer. Why, the whole contract from beginning to end differentiates the conditions on which the mountain section and the prairie section are to be constructed. Take, for instance, the terms of the guarantee. There is one state of things provided in regard to the mountain section and an entirely different state as regards the prairie section. These two sections must of necessity be constructed independently. So far apart are they from each other in every respect that they might well be constructed by two distinct companies. It is absolutely essential that every dollar expended on the one section should be kept distinct from that spent on the other, so that we may know what the cost of each may be. Yet the hon. gentleman, so anxious is he that the whole western division should be one entire system without any possible distinction or difference between them, that he must insist even that the contract time limit for the two sections of that division shall be the same ! I cannot believe that the hon. gentleman was serious. Does his right hon. leader say that it was because of any regard for the harmonies of that beautiful contract that 711
he could not ask any difference in the conditions as regards the time for construction in each case ? No, the right hon. gentleman was actuated by other motives. To him it was a question of whether the company would be able to find labour. These hon. gentlemen do not seem to go upon the same ground. There seems to be uo common thought between them with regard to this most important contract. But does the right hon. gentleman mean to tell this House that the Grand Trunk Company asked eight years to construct the prairie section because they would not be able to get labour ? If that is what the right hon. gentleman wants this House to understand, I should like to know it. I think the people of the Northwest would like to know whether the First Minister advanced as a reason for allowing the company eight years in which to build that prairie section that they would not be able to get labour. But that is the only answer which the right hon. gentleman has given us. The Minister of Justice deals with the harmonies and the right hon. gentleman deals with the practical question of labour.
Now, what is the fact '< In the original agreement five years had been allowed the Grand Trunk Pacific in which to build the western division. I speak of it as the Grand Trunk Railway Company. We need not trouble to specify the Grand Trunk Pacific. They are the same. The Grand Trunk Railway Company asked the ministers for three additional years. I do not suppose that anybody in the House would have made any great complaint about allowing them eight years for the completion of the mountain section. But when the Grand Trunk Company asked the government to change the time limit of construction of the western division from five to eight years, did the government ask the Grand Trunk their reason for making that request 7 I presume hon. gentlemen on the treasury benches would not at once bow to such a request from the Grand Trunk Company. I presume the right hon. Prime Minister and his colleagues would ask the reason why the extension should be granted-any business man, under similar circumstances, would put such a question. And I have no doubt that the answer would have been : We cannot construct the mountain section in five years. And what would be the natural reply of the government to that 7 It would be : Well, take eight years for the mountain section, but it does not follow that you should have eight years for the prairie section ; we will grant the extension as to the mountain section, but we will leave the contract where it is as to the line over the prairies. Is .it not clear that is what hon. gentlemen would have done had they been considering the interest of the people who occupy the Northwest 7 But that is not what the Prime Minister

and Ills colleagues did. When this request for three more years was made, they bowed and submitted-that is all. I cannot understand what they were thinking of that they did not at once say : We will grant eight years for the mountain section, but, in the interest of the people in the Northwest, we cannot grant you such an extension for the prairie section. Why did the government grant this extension of time over the whole division ? That is a question asked by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche) and, up to this time, we have had no answer, no possible excuse presented. Why, in contrast with the work done on some portions of tli? Canadian Pacific Railway this building of a railway across the prairie is mere child's play. You can construct a mile a day without trouble ; and'if there had been all the urgency that hon. gentlemen opposite imagined last year, even a mile a day would have been nothing to men who wanted to meet that urgency. But, so anxious were the government to make an agreement, they did not pause to consider, when tills request of the Grand Trunk was submitted, that it might be reasonable to grant it for one section of the division and not for the other. No, they gave the Grand Trunk Company what they asked without a moment's consideration. In giving his answer here, the Prime Minister has not pretended for a moment to give a reason for this extension of time as regards the prairie section. Every time he referred to the subject, he spoke of the western division-the whole 1,500 miles, 1,000 miles to be constructed over a tableland and 500 miles through the mountains. And they allowed the Grand Trunk to have thei same time for construction of the line across the table-land as for the other. British Columbia wants the mountain section built soon. But I have no doubt that they would be willing, as reasonable people, to grant eight years for the completion of that mountain work. But what about the people of the Northwest who, hon. gentlemen say are pressing for relief ? Why allow 'the company to keep them waiting for eight years ? Why grant this extension as to the mountain section without even a word being said in favour of more rapid construction of the prairie section? I think that is a very important question to be answered in this House to-night. It is important for this reason-and I desire to bring this particularly, to the attention of the right hon. gentleman, and of the country, and more particularly to the attention of the people of the Northwest-if the right hon. gentleman and his government had not interposed last year when the Grand Trunk proposed to build the line from the Pacific to North Bay, the work of construction on the prairie section would be going on at this moment ! But not a sod has been turned. There is no reason why the work of construction on the prairie sectiqn should not have been com-Mr. BARKER.
menced last August, and we could have had a good deal of that road in operation at this moment. But the right hon. gentleman saw the opportunity for a great political coup, which induced him to interfere with the project of the Grand Trunk. And, in consequence of that interference, the people of the Northwest are to-day just where they were a year ago as regards this most urgent and pressing matter. Now, Sir, 1 say that we are entitled to know from the right hon. gentleman, in definite and specific terms, whah it was that induced him to agree to the extension of the time for the construction, not as regards the western division, but as regards the prairie section of the western division. It was to that that the question of the hon. member tor Marquette was directed, and to that only. But, every time that the Prime Minister purported to answer tha,t question, he carefully avoided saying one word about the section ; it was always about the western division, as if it were impossible to distinguish between the two sections of that division. And yet, these two sections are distinctly and differ ently dealt with from beginning to end. Whien the right hon. gentleman entered into arrangements to give a specific and particular subsidy for the mountain section and another for the prairie section why should he not also have arranged as to the time of construction of these two sections V Surely they can be as easily distinguished on one point as on the other. But it never occurred to him ; that is quite apparent, and they quietly concurred in the request of the Grand Trunk. And so it has been from the beginning to the end of this supplemental agreement. Everything has been most cautiously and carefully stipulated for on behalf of the Grand Trunk-and cleverly stipulated, be it said to the great credit of the officers of that company-and not a word in the interests of the people. That is why the question asked by the hon. member for Marquette calls for an answer, and a specific answer by the Prime Minister. It is not merely that the prairie section has been delayed by the interposition of the government, by their interference with a private Bill introduced into this House by parties who were willing to undertake this great work, but we see not the slightest exertion on the) part of the government to advance the project that they themselves have fathered. What about this eastern division ?
The hon. the Minister of the Interior had to admit in his place in this House that it was to be regretted that we were not in possession of the plans and surveys. The Grand Trunk Railway, with their usual alertness, are not altogether without plans and surveys. They are to-day. and have been for months in the past year, surveying the very section through which the government are undertaking to construct a railway. They have been spending large sums of

money in surveying that section and tiie government have actually not turned a finger in promotion of what caused the right lion, gentleman such anxiety in July last. He has not given an order, he has not employed a surveyor or an engineer, nothing has been done. Everything that has been done has been done by the Grand Trunk, and according to the right hon. gentleman they are doing it at their own expense, they are doing the work of tire government of Canada and the right hon. gentleman would have us believe that there is no understanding whatever that they are going to be repaid for the expense. Well, we are bound to have a good deal of faith, parliamentary faith, but I do not believe that there is a man in this country who believes that there is no implied understanding-I do not say express understanding ; I can quite believe that there has not been a word between the right hon. gentleman and the general manager and second vice-president of the Grand Trunk on the subject-but I believe there is not a man from one end of Canada to the other who believes that there is not a perfect tacit understanding between them that every dollar expended by the Grand Trunk iu surveying the route over which the government has undertaken to construct a railway will be repaid to the Grand Trunk, and yet this House, which has to act on behalf of the people of Canada in deciding these questions, is to be deprived until too late for action of the information for Which the people's money will sooner or later pay. That is the position. I say that such questions as that put by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche) should receive serious consideration from the government and a reply so explicit that hereafter there may be no misunderstanding about it. We want to know, on behalf of the people of Canada and especially on behalf of the people of the Northwest, on what ground the Grand Trunk Railway Company asked that the time for the completion of the prairie section should be extended to eight years, and on what ground the right hon. gentleman assented to that request.
SIR WILFRID CARRIER. After having listened carefully to the remarks of my hon. friend from Hamilton. I am convinced that I cannot satisfy him by anything I say or anything I do not say. When we were negotiating with the Grand Trunk Railway Company I had all the time before my eyes, I must admit, the power of obstruction that can be developed by the opposition. I must confess that, much as I knew of their powers of quibbling and pettifogging I was never within the mark ; I never realized that the powers of pettifogging and quibbling could be carried as far as they have just been carried by the hon. gentleman.

Does the right hon. gentleman mean that the observations I have made are pettifogging ?
SIR WILFRID LAURIER. I do.

You do ?
SIR WILFRID LAURIER. Yes.

I will not attempt to characterize the conduct of the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) ; my remarks would not be within the rules of this House.
SIR WILFRID LAURIER. It is quite possible that the observations of the hon. gentleman would not be parliamentary, but mine are : that is the difference between him and me, and I tell him the speech he has just made is mere quibbling and pettifogging and nothing else. The hon. gentleman would have us think of possible objections which no man of common sense, entering upon a bargain such as this, would ever think of. The hon. gentleman finds no fault because we extended the time given to the Grand Trunk Pacific for eight years in so far as the mountain section is concerned. The hon. gentleman admits that he and his friends would be willing to permit an extension of time for the mountain section, but he says : What about the prairie section ? Does he believe that we thought that all parts of the mountain section and of the prairie section would be completed at the same time ? We thought that some parts of the road would be built before the others, and that the prairie section would be built before the mountain section. The prairie section must be built first, and therefore if it was not improper of the Grand Trunk to ask an extension for eight years for the mountain section, it is quite possible that there is practically no extension for the prairie section. It goes without saying that the prairie section would be built first, and therefore there was no reason to limit the time for the completion of the prairie section. It went as a matter of course that the prairie section would be built first, and in regard to this I rely on the common sense of every man in this House. If this is not understood by every man, I call it nothing more than quibbling and pettifogging to question it. I have been told in this House again and again, that I am not a business man.

Hear, hear.
SIR WILFRID LAURIER. I do not pretend that I am, but when I hear the assertions of some of the men who pose as business men, when I see the assumptions put forward by some men posing as business men, why, Sir. I am surprised at my own modesty. When we made this contract we did not think of things except what a reasonable man would think of, and we never thought of what a quibbler and pettifogger would think of. Therefore. Sir, the hon. gentleman must understand that whilst we are prepared to give him every satisfac-' tion in reference to every reasonable objec-

tion anti to answer his reasonable questions, lie cannot expect that when he wants to obstruct under the name of discussing legal objections we shall answer his argument.

The crossing from this side of the House to the opposite side and his installation as Prime Minister has brought out an attribute in the Premier which he was not known to possess, a temper. When the hon. gentleman was in opposition, no matter how hard the blows rained from ministerial benches on his followers, he never came to their rescue and he never attempted to castigate anybody. But, Sir, he has assumed a new role of late, and one can see he is rather smarting under the castigation he received from the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) last night. However, we have one thing from the First Minister, and that is that he disclaims being a business man, and I am sure the Minister of Justice will have to make a similar confession if no other reasons can be adduced for the extension of time for three years for the building of the prairie section. This section will be about 1,000 miles in length, and we were told in the committee room a year ago by Mr. Hays and Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson that when this work was commenced it would be carried on and expedited in a way that would dazzle the people of Canada. The puny, pigmy efforts of the Canadian Pacific Railway were to be outclassed. Mr. Hays said they would bring to the building of the road that superior equipment of the Grand Trunk before which everything would have to wither and quail as grain before a cyclone.
And yet what is the admission to-night ?- that this powerful organization is unable to go into that country and attempt to perform what the Canadian Pacific Railway did some years ago. As pointed out by my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) there have been two reasons assigned and they are as different and as far apart as the poles. The hon. Minister of Justice was a little more fertile in his resources and his imagination when lie put up his reasons. His reason, in the first place, was that it was not necessary to compel a man in law to do anything which he was bound to do and it was aptly suggested to the hon. gentleman that he had better tear up the agreement altogether. Does the hon.
