Minister of Justice expect that any common sense man will believe that they extended the time simply because they knew that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company would not take advantage of it ? As to the reason given by the right hon. First Minister I can only say that while I do not pose as a railway expert at all, I have seen some works of railway constructed in this country and if the right hon. gentleman, some day in passing a work of railway construction, will deign to look at those who are performing the work he will find that they are not Canadians or Americans but Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
that they are Italians, Poles, and other foreigners of the same kind, and as his colleague the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton) has been so kind as to import a great many Doukhobors, Galicians and other pet friends of the hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis), there cannot be a doubt that there will be almost myriads of these foreigners in that country ready to perform that labour.
The hon. gentleman should issue an epistle to the Galicians.

Perhaps the hoii. gentleman could issue an epistle to them interspersed with blanks. What is the difference between the conditions existing at the time the Canadian Pacific Railway was constructed and those which will confront the Grand Trunk Pacific to-day in the work of constructioin ? When the Canadian Pacific Railway commenced their march westward from Winnipeg there was not a single railway track upon which they could carry one pound of their supplies. Their equipment had to follow up as the work of construction progressed. Here, the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company commence with the advantage that for over half of the distance, for over 1,000 miles, their line runs almost parallel with the Canadian Northern system. They can take the magnificent equipment of the Grand Trunk Railway Company proper out of Ontario and the older iiro-vinces, they can take their locomotives and cars and run them over the Canadian Pacific Railway and after leaving Winnipeg they can proceed by either the Canadian Northern Railway or the Canadian Pacific Railway with their equipment while the work of construction is going on. But, more than that and better than tliat, when the Canadian Pacific Railway was being constructed, the company were not in a position to forward one pound of the supplies beyond the end of their track. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company have placed before the public a certain map outlining a certain route which they propose to follow. Look at the superior position, that vantage ground they have to-day. If the right hon. First Minister will only look at the ordinary printed folder of the Canadian Pacific Railway he will see the superior advantages that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company are to have. First and foremost they can reach Winnipeg by 'the Canadian Northern or the Canadian Pacific Railway and start their work at a dozen different points on a line paralleled by the Canadian Pacific Railway. Nay. more than that, they can go on the line of the Canadian Pacific Railway as far as Regina and then take the line between Regina and Prince Albert, they can start and work from there eastward and in that way meet their line which is building from the east to the west. But, not only have they the advantage of being able to send

their equipment from Winnipeg out to a point north of Regina and then working from Regina towards Winnipeg and both working to the centre, as it were, but they have this further advantage that they can go as far as Calgary with their construction trains, then go north to Edmonton and start working from Edmonton westward. Here is a railway which has the Grand Trunk Railway Company behind it, and the company have an advantage in the matter of construction in that way. In to-day's ' Globe ' there is an interview with Mr. Wm. Mackenzie, of the Canadian Northern Railway Company, and Mr. Mackenzie, interviewed at Winnipeg, makes the statement that the Canadian Northern Railway Company are going to build no less than 600 miles of road this season-no less than GOO miles in a single season. Yet, the right lion. Prime Minister is tacitly admitting that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company cannot do the work at a quicker rate than 300 miles per year. This little effort of the Canadian Northern Railway Company of 600 miles a year is a greater undertaking, than, apparently, the government imagine this company can accomplish. Look at the superior advantages they will have compared with those which the Canadian Pacific Railway bad. The country north of Edmonton is being opened up. It is a timber country ; it abounds with spruce. Bringing in the ties was one of the greatest difficulties that the Canadian Pacific Railway had to contend with in the construction of their road, because, I think that most of the ties were taken from a point east of Winnipeg or in that direction. The Grand Trunk Pacific can take their ties from Edmonton. They can be floated down the river and taken in to the different points where this line of railway will be under construction. The fact of the matter is that the government hope to temporize with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company and they do not want to force them to do what the country expects. During the course of this debate, as also during the debate of last year, it was openly asserted that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company expected for many years to come, not to have to construct the line on the north shore of lake Superior and that it was not the intention to require the Grand Trunk Pacific for many years to even construct the line to the head of lake Superior. It was asserted that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company could build their line westward from Winnipeg and then from Winnipeg they could extend their line to Emerson and by making connection with American lines they could send their grain out by way of Duluth. More than that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company will be in this position that they need not keep on extending their main line in a westerly direction but that instead of going in a westerly direction they can build their brarieh lines and use their capital for extending their laterals north and south of their main line. This is a matter of some local interest to the constituency which I represent. We have been told that this railway is going to be a great benefit to the province of Ontario. We have been told that all these towns, Midland, Collingwood, Goderich and the rest of them are to reap certain advantages. If we are to reap them, let us have them at the earliest period possible. Let us force this company to build this line with the least possible delay and bring their grain down at once whether they bring it to Duluth or a point on the head of Lake Superior. It is rather amusing to see these hon. gentlemen from the Northwest on the government side of the House who have been crying out for the last six or seven years for railway accommodation are the very first to throw a wet blanket over the proposition that this railway should be forced through to Edmonton in the quickest time possible. Edmonton is the end of the prairie section. We have had this afternoon the experiences of hon. gentlemen who lived in the province of Manitoba during the period of the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway and we have had the statement from them that the Canadian Pacific Railway with all its disadvantages and drawbacks was built at the rate of one mile a day and even faster. I have been informed that prairie railways can be built at the rate of from three to five miles a day. Superior appliances are to be had now. Whereas in years gone by track laying was done by hand there is machinery now for that purpose and there cannot be a doubt that this railway can be forced through, not in five or eight years, but that the work can be done even in from two to three years. And yet, the government, for reasons, best known to themselves, are interposing conditions between the settlers of the Northwest and the construction of this railway which will retard its; completion for several years. The people of the west now see that men like my hon. friend from Macdonald (Mr. Boyd) and from Marquette (Mr. W. J. Roche) are their real champions, and not the Liberal members from the Northwest who support whatever the Prime Minister may propose.

I regret that the Prime Minister has lost that control over himself that he usually possesses : I regret that the right hon. gentleman did not rise in that dignified manner which becomes the Prime Minister of a nation which he created in a night. Indeed, Sir, I regret that he did oeate this Canadian nation so rapidly, because he might better have taken a little more time, and pared off some of the defects which he and the government are responsible for, and which the people of Canada have reason to deplore. The right hon. gentleman has described the arguments used by hon. members on this side, as pettifogging. That term may be parlia-

u.entary, but it is not polite, and it does not carry with it much conviction. The contract made last session and torn up, and the contract made this session and whicu may be torn up again, are enough to indicate to the people of Canada just exactly where they may seek pettifoggers, if they want to find them. I would ask the right hon. gentleman-not that 1 expect him +o answer-have we not a right on this side of' the House to be inquisitive, in view of the broken promises and pledges anent this contract with the Grand Trunk Railway, which have been made by himself and his colleagues. If the Prime Minister's argument was not pettifogging, it ought to be as good this year as it was last year. He told us last year, that we could not afford to wait: that he had no patience with the man who .would say : ,to-morrow, and tomorrow ; but we have waited for several to morrows, and we are still waiting, and e\ en though I should run the risk of incurring Itliie anger of the Prime i'MJinister, I tell him, that acting in the interests of the people of Canada, I will fight against this contract just as long as I can. If the right hon. gentleman thinks that by calling us pettifoggers or demagogues or any other ' gogs.' he will scare us from our defence of the public interests, he is making a mighty big mistake. Under our constitution, one man is selected to be the B'irst Minister of the government of the day, but even though he holds that high and honourable position, he must remember that he never ceases to be a common member of parliament. just the same as, the rest of us. He can dictate to his own followers and he can make them do as he pleases, but he has no right to dictate to the free and independent members on this side of the House ; and the sooner he learns that the better. In the speech delivered by Sir Rivers-Wilson, we find the following statement:
As a result, however, of negotiations with the government another Bill was introduced by the government itself for insuring the construction of the contemplated line from New Brunswick to the Pacific in joint partnership between the government and the Grand Trunk Pacific Company.
I have already stated that such a partnership was an immoral partnership. We have a partnership here between the government of Canada and a private corporation, both being jointly and severally interested, and how can we expect the government to make an independent bargain in the interests of the people of Canada, with their co-partners the Grand Trunk Railway Company ? The moment that that partnership was signed, no longer was there an independent government, and no longer was the government able to protect the rights of the people. The immorality of that partnership will be demonstrated time and time again, and If I mistake not the courts of tlie country will furnish us with plenty of Mr. POPE.
evidence in the days to come, of the immorality of that partnership between the government of Canada and the Grand Tiunk Railway Company, which has only a mercantile sordid interest in the transaction. We need not expect to find patriotism in the Grand Trunk Company ; they are after the almighty dollar. The right lien, gentleman has linked himself with a corporation that has only the one desire, namely to make money, to make it fast, and to make all they can out of Canada. Wlierv is the Minister of Railways and Canals to defend this contract ? Day In and day out, he has sat in his seat, engaging the Minister of the Interior and the Prime Minister and a few others to defend a measure which belongs to his department, and he is no more use than
Last year's bird's nest.

Yes, thank you for the word. There never was such a spectacle before in a parliament, and there never will he such a spectacle again. Mocked at by his own party, mocked at by the people of the country, mocked at by the press of the country, ridiculed and snuffed at out of sight, there never was such a spectacle and I trust there never will be again. The Minister of Railways and Canals has at his command engineers of great experience, numbers of men operating a railway, and he ought to he able to bring to bear the great experience of his department to explain this contract, but he is silent as the grave.
Notwithstanding the pettifogging argument of the hon. member for Hamilton, I am going to venture, even iff the presence of that august gentleman who sits as the Prime Minister of-Canada, to say that the contract is weak in permitting the company to take eight years in the work of construction. But the right hon. gentleman says they are not going to take eight years. If not. why not put that in the contract ? The people of Canada would then feel that the right hon. gentleman and his government were more keenly alive to the public interests. The whole product of the prairie country does not go eastward ; a great deal of it goes westward ; and even to pierce the mountains eight years is a long time. The products of the prairie country that go to the Pacific coast are increasing every year. The people of the section around Edmonton are importers of wheat, as they grow less thau they consume. They have great oatmeal mills, the product of which goes to the Pacific, and from there to different parts of the world. We have been for years urging on this government the speedy development of that country by the construction of railways ; and the necessity of doing something never seemed to dawn on their minds until the hour arrived when some man could not wait, whose name was mentioned

to us last year by tlie ex-Minister of Railways and Canals on the occasion of his retirement. As the right lion, gentleman knows, the surveys through that country were made by the government In days gone by, and those surveys will now become the property of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, so that the construction of the railway could go on there without delay. I believe that we are making an honest plea in the best interests of the prairie section. I have no doubt that the hon. gentlemen who come here from that country will say : We have confidence that the company will build it earlier.
Certainly.

If the hon. gentleman were making a contract with me for a work that I could do in three years, would he make the time eight years? Not at all. He would say: If you can do it in three years, let the contract say three years. The people of Canada are paying a high price for this road by guaranteeing three-fourths of the cost in order that we may have that rapid construction ; and when they do that, they have as much right to have terms written as the Grand Trunk Pacific Company. But in this contract you will find no clause written in the interest of the people of Canada. Every clause is written in the interest of the Grand Trunk Pacific.
They cannot reap any benefit until they begin hauling traffic from the prairies to the lakes.
It is not going to take you eight years to build to the lakes. How long were Mackenzie & Mann in building from Winnipeg to the lakes ?
They are building yet.
How long were they building ?
About four years.

That is not absolutely correct. The hon. gentleman is now proving my case. Making allowance for statements made by lion, gentlemen opposite, it was probably two years or two and a-half years at the outside. That is the way we have to discount statements made by these hon. gentlemen. The company could carry on the work of construction all along the line as far west as Edmonton. The supplies could be carried in by the Canadian Pacific Railway.
Does the hon. gentleman know how much the Canadian Pacific Railway charged the Canadian Northern Company for carrying one locomotive to Edmonton ? About what the locomotive was worth.

Yes, and I will guarantee that the Canadian Pacific Railway will make a contract with the Grand Trunk Pacific to carry in supplies at as low a rate as they would for me. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company intend to make money out of this railway, and they are not fools. They will take the opportunity of carrying then-freight, and make money out of it. There is no comparison between the conditions under which the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian Northern Railway were built. If you consult Mr. Hays or Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson, or any other man connected with the Grand Trunk, you will find that they estimate that the opportunity for speedy construction in that country is to-day far better than it ever was.
Certainly.
Then, why not put in one clause for the people of Canada ?
Why not pass the Bill, and let them go to work ?
You stopped them for two years.

Why, the contract was only introduced last July, and it went into force, so far as this House was concerned, in October. Under these circumstances, how can the hon. gentleman say-, when the government found they had to amend the contract, and when they went into this immoral partnership, that we kept back the work for two years ? That is just about as true as the hon. gentleman's statement that it took four years to build the Canadian Northern road from Winnipeg to the great lakes. That is about the style of argument put up by these hon. gentlemen. What has become of those gentlemen who were clamouring for speedy development of that country some y-ears ago. and appealing for additional railway facilities ? They are to-day as silent as the tomb. Not one word of protest dare they utter against this proposition to retard the construction of this prairie section three years longer than the time provided in the original contract. So thoroughly whipped into line have they been, that, far from being pettifoggers, they dare not call their souls their own. Sir, what would have become of that country had it not been for the Conservative party ? We cannot find a railway existing in the Northwest, except the Crow's Nest Pass Railway, which was not promoted by a Conservative administration.
What about the Canadian Northern ? That was not heard of in the time of the late government.

The Canadian Northern never built a mile in the Territories until this year, and then it received the unanimous support of this side of the House. There has not been a spike driven in any railway in the Territories which has not had the faithful support of hon. gentlemen on this side, whether they were the governing body-or in opposition. When hon. gentlemen opposite are not in a position to make any- such claim, they take credit for railway construc-I tion and development in that great western

world. We know their past history. We know the past history of the right hon. gentleman who leads this House. We know the position that he took in former days on railway construction in that country, and we have the admission to-day by any number of Liberals in the country and by some hon. gentlemen on the government benches that the Liberal party then followed a mistaken policy. If hon. gentlemen opposite want to show any independence and any desire to benefit their country, let them give us some evidence of it on this clause of the contract. I have no doubt that the First Minister acted in the best of faith, but the moment we confirm this supplemental agreement, we are enabling the Grand Trunk Railway to hold back the railway development of the Northwest. Even five years is too long a time to take to build that prairie section. That railway should be built from the great lakes to Edmouton in three yekr's time at the very furthest. Why not put a condition to that effect in the contract? The right hon. the Prime Minister himself gave us last session to understand that there was danger ahead if we did not have speedy construction of this road. He said that no one could tell what the morrow might bring forward, and it was on his personal pledge to this House that we would have a speedy construction of this railway, that his followers agreed to accept the contract. But now he is having the time limit extended three years, and we on this side ask him to consider the solemn promise he made last year, and compel this corporation to construct that prairie section within reasonable time, say. three or four years. But when we urge this view upon the right hon. gentleman, instead of attempting to argue, he charges us with being pettifoggers. How dare hon. gentlemen on the other side, he exclaims, so far forget themselves as to talk pettifogging nonsense in the presence of myself, the Prime Minister ?
The right hon. gentleman has laid great stress on the prospect that the people in the east will be well repaid in the shape of cheap freight rates on the manufactured goods they send to the west. Well, does not the right hon. gentleman see that that plea turns against himself ? Undoubtedly there is no time in the history of the settler when he so much requires cheap goods as when he has started in a new country, with but little money and has to meet all the conditions which make success difficult. But here we have the right hon. gentleman retarding by three years that desired period, when the completion of tills projected railway across the prairies will give cheaper rates of freight.
Then take the North Bay section. We have no promise from the government when the eastern section is going to begin. We have no promise from the government that they are going to push through that section Mr. POPE.
at an early date. From North Bay to Winnipeg will be an important feeder for the Brand Trunk Railway. It has been stated over and over again that the Grand Trunk Railway cannot utilize the prairie section until they get to North Bay so as to make connection with their eastern lines. Consequently the construction of the line to North Bay is essential to the west as well as to the east ; yet we have no information as to when that will be begun.
I notice that in the speech made last year by the right hon. gentleman he took pains to refer to the amendment which he proposed when the Bill to incorporate the Canadian Pacific Railway was before the House. At that time he said
Iu the opinion of this House, additional surveys are requisite in order to come to a sound decision for the short line railway, and it would be premature to adopt any line before further surveys have been made.
If that argument was good then, it is good to-day. The right hon. gentleman shakes his head.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The conditions are not parallel at all.
In what particular ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The project then was to build a short line through the state of Maine.
And the right hon. gentleman wanted surveys.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Before going through a foreign country.

Why, the hills and mountains and dales were made by nature, and they are just the same whether they happen to be in the state of Maine or the province of New Brunswick. That section of road through the state of Maine was a rough section just as is the section through the maritime provinces. When you leave Quebec and run north, you have a difficult country suih as was described by that missionary some 250 years ago. He took a diagonal course in his journey. He started from Saguenay and went to Lake St. John, where he wintered and from Lake St. John he went to James Bay. That is not the route to be traversed, it is a route to be crossed, somewhat diagonally, by the road coming up from Quebec. If you take a description of that journey as read here the other night, you will see that the traveller refers to a mountainous region with waterfalls, and he tells of the difficulties he encounters in making progress. If that is the section to be gone through, I say there cannot be haste, if we are to observe the principle of the resolution of the right hon. gentleman of some years ago. And this country is in Canada ; it is not under the American flag ; and consequently it has not been interfered with since the missionary was there two

hundred and fifty years ago. Traversing that section of the country we find ourselves making our way to a point opposite North Bay, where the Grand Trunk Company intend to build a branch from the government road to North Bay. Then you travel on to Winnipeg. We know the difficulties that the Canadian Pacific Railway encountered between North Bay and Winnipeg. And nobody has any information today-if there is any information it ought to be on that table ; it has no right to be anywhere else when this question is being discussed-that would warrant the assertion that this road from North Bay to Winnipeg can be constructed for one dollar less than it cost to build the Canadian Pacific Railway from North Bay to Winnipeg. There may be greater difficulties even-we do not know. Under these conditions, it is important that the government should say to us when they are going to begin this eastern section ; when they are going to begin the construction from North Bay to Winnipeg, in order to give the Grand Trunk connection with their line in the east; and when they are going to begin the construction from North Bay to Quebec and from Quebec to Moncton. But the right bon. gentleman says we are pettifoggers. Why are we pettifoggers ? We are asking for the same information that he asked for in this resolution, information that he said he ought to have even before a route was selected, to say nothing of making a promise to build a road. But before parliament might even vote that money should be spent in a country similar to this-except that part of it was in the United States-he demanded that a survey should be made. And, forsooth, though he made that statement eighteen years! ago and quoted it in his speech last year, and because we to-day hesitate to vote $175,000,000 of the people's money to build through a region that has never, been surveyed, he says we are pettifoggers. The hon. gentleman refers us to his so-called ' mountains of information.' He refers us to the book of the old missionary of two hundred and fifty years ago. And when we read that book, every line of it condemns, as the hon. gentleman's own resolution condemns, the action of this government in deciding to spend $175,000,000 of the people's money without securing further information.

At the risk of being called a pettifogger and quibbler and other nice names by the Prime Minister of this country-names that go down in our records and will stand as examples to future generations of the parliamentary language used by the Prime Minister of our country at this time-I am going to ask a few questions of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice who are jointly in charge of this Bill before the House. It may be that by asking them in a more humble way and
with less force than was thought necessary by my respected colleague and friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) I may get back to the sunny ways that were supposed to characterize us in this House, when that expression was used to describe the hon. gentleman who was not then Prime Minister, but was hoping to be. And, from these sunny ways, we may get some sunshine thrown upon the darkness of this contract, so that the ordinary people of Canada may understand it.
I do not know exactly what a pettifogger or a quibbler is. We do not grow such things among the peach trees and grape vines of the county of Lincoln. But I imagine, from the expression on the face of the Prime Minister when using the words, that they are not very nice things. The Prime Minister looked as if he thought he was saying something nasty and something offensive. I am going to try and get along without saying anything that will bring that expression to his face when answering me. One question that I would like to have answered is the question! put by my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. W. J. Roche), the question that we have been trying to get an answer to all afternoon-why, when the mountain section is differentiated from the prairie section in regard to the subsidies and the guarantee, it is to be counted as pettifogging and quibbling when we desire to know why they cannot be differentiated as to time of construction ? Now, I desire to point out one or two things in this contract to the Prime Minister-who may not have read the contract ; I do not know whether he has read it or not. In section 15 of the contract, which is just before the signature, it is agreed :-
This agreement shall be submitted to and be subject to ratification by the parliament ot Canada.
We are in the parliament of Canada now and we are asked to ratify this contract. We must ratify it before it can become effective even though it has been signed by the Minister of Railways and Canals-who appears to have been afraid of it ever since. The first thing in this agreement is that the time of construction is to be extended. The original contract is being amended in this respect, and we must read the original contract before we can understand this provision. Section 4 of the contract deals with the western section. It will not take me very long to read it, and I think I must read it to the Prime Minister to show him what it is he is calling pettifogging and quibbling. This section) provides :-
4. The said western division is further, for convenient reference, considered as being divided into sections, one extending from the eastern terminus thereof westerly to the eastern limit of the Rocky mountains (herein designated as the ' prairie section '), and the other extending westerly from the said eastern limit of the Rocky mountains to the western

224S
terminus of the said division (herein designated as the ' mountain section '). The said eastern limit of the Rocky mountains shall be established after the location of the line, and after actual surveys have determined the profile thereof upon such location, and shall be fixed and agreed upon by the chief engineer of the company and the chief engineer of the government as the result of such surveys, having regard to the physical features of the country, and to the cost of construction, and endeavouring as fairly as possible to determine where the more easy and less expensive work characteristic of prairie construction comes to an end, and the more difficult and expensive work characteristic of mountain construction begins, and, in case the said engineers shall differ, the question shall be determined by the said engineers and a third arbitrator, to be chosen by them, in the event of their inability to agree on a third arbitrator, the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Canada may appoint the said third arbitrator, and the decision of the majority shall be final. .
Special provision is made in order to determine where the prairie section begins and where the mountain section ends. Is it pettifogging and quibbling for these gentlemen to go to all this trouble to make a distinction between the mountain section and the prairie section ? And are we properly to be called pettifoggers and quibblers because we ask why no distinction is made between these two sections in respect of the time of construction 7 When we say that the part which costs less than the other should be built earlier than the more expensive part 7 The Prime Minister talks about common sense. That is a word that I am not so unfamiliar with as with 'pettifogging' and ' quibbling.'	[DOT]
I have heard the words * common sense ' used once or twice in this House, and the Prime Minister found no common sense in the question of the hon. member for Hamil-tcn (Mr. Barker). I can tell the Prime Minister that the people of the county of Lincoln, and people who used to support the Prime Minister, are asking me this question every time they can catch me, and asking why we cannot induce the government to change the contract so that the gi eat wheat fields of the west can be tapped earlier than the mountain section. If we are pettifogging and quibbling and not talking common sense, the people of Canada, whom we represent, are quibbling an# pettifogging and not talking common sense to the members who represent them in this House. The whole people of Canada are asking that question and expect the members of the Dominion parliament where the contract is being sought to be perfected, to induce the government to give some satisfactory reason, if any exists, for not making this stipulation. What was the answer of the Minister of Justice, for instance, to the reasons advanced why this distinction should be made, and an earlier time fixed for the constructon of the prairie section than of the mountain section, instead of Mr. LANCASTER.
treating it all as one section ? He said that different clauses of the contract would not harmonize. He also said the company could be depended upon to commence operations as soon as possible, that the business was there waiting for them, I do not suppose any one would have been justified in accusing the Minister of Justice of quibbling and pettifogging in giving these answers, but I must say they are not such answers as should have been given to members on this side, and it will be inferred by the people of this country that the reason he gave them was that there was no better answer to give. This matter was not thought of in making the contract, it never entered the mind of the government until the members of the opposition asked a question, but instead of being frank enough to stand up and say : that never occurred tr us, we will do our best, although we have signed the contract, and have really no power over the Grand Trunk left, to get them to build the prairie section first and thus accomplish, in a roundabout way, what we could have accomplished in a direct way, if we had thought of it in time. The Minister of Justice has suggested that they can be depended upon to build the prairie section first, and as to the quality of the road, they know very well what the contract means and so it does not matter to us. For instance when w e are told that the contract calls for a road of equal quality with the Grand Trunk between Montreal and Toronto, the Minister of Justice, being asked what sort of road that would mean, answered that the Grand Trunk knew what the contract meant in that respect, he was not a railway builder, and did not know. Now, that is not pettifogging or quibbling, I do not say it is, but it is not answering the question in such a way as to satisfy the people of this country, whom we represent. That is not an answer that will clear up the anxiety of the people. It would have been more fair if the Prime Minister had turned to the Minister of Justice and said : if you go on answering in that way, I shall have to accuse you of pettifogging and quibbling. The Prime Minister knows well that the Northwestern members insist upon clauses of the most stringent character being inserted in every Bill for the construction of railways through the prairies providing for the immediate building of the lines authorized. Everything must be done at once in the prairie section. Hon. gentlemen from the prairie section on both sides of this House, have joined hands in this demand, but why is it that the Liberal mem bers from the west are not supporting their colleagues on this side^ of the House in urging the government'T'or a more speedy construction of this prairie section. Is it because they have been called pettifoggers and quibblers, or accused of not talking common sense ? Or is it because they do

not like the expression on the premier's face when such a question is asked and is that why his majority was cut to 19 the other day ? The people of Canada want some other answer than that. Those reformers who. voted for me at the last election and who are going to vote for me at the next election, because they believe that the government has not lived up to their pledges, will want some other answer. They know that the government have broken all their pledges, but they have thought they had still the sunny ways to fall back upon. They do not want me to tell them that the premier is always angry and will not answer the questions of the opposition without flying into a passion. I want to be able to tell them that no matter to what party the premier belongs he is still a Canadian, and a courteous man, and one who will not call the members names. I wish to call attention to a matter referred to by the member for Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee), which was received in utter silence and was apparently considered altogether below the notice of this government. The member for Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee) pointed out the effect of the position of the word ' strikes ' in the first section of the contract. I do not wish to repeat what the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee) said, but I wish to reiterate his idea, because it seems that he was not able to speak loudly enough to attract the attention of the Prime Minister to his case or else his subject was not of sufficient importance to this country to receive any notice or even to obtain a scolding for the hon. gentleman for having raised it. He pointed out that the insertion of the word ' strikes ' in this contract might have the effect of giving the Grand Trunk a very easy excuse for breaking the contract.
They can treat their labourers employed upon the construction of the road in such a way as to bring on a strike. They can treat them in such a way that no labourers, no matter how good natured they might be, could endure it, with the result that a strike would be brought about, and in that way they could break the contract with impunity. There is no provision in this contract by which any tribunal shall decide whether a strike which may occur is a bona fide strike or the fault of the company or not. There is no provision made by the government should anything happen, to protect them against the necessity of submitting to any conditions which the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company choose to impose. They can say : We have a strike, as a result of which this contract is at an end ; we are under no penalty, and you cannot do anything to us. That is a matter which ought to have been considered. The hon. member for Winnipeg (Sir. Puttee), representing, perhaps, in a little more special degree than the rest of us, the labour interests
1 of this country, was certainly within his rights in drawing the attention of the gov-eminent to that matter, and I think the government ought to have given some answer in | regard to it. He also mentioned the fact that i alien labour might be brought in if a strike did take place ; yet the government have not answered that point at all. I wish to point cut that when it suits the right hon. Prime Minister to use the labour question to show how certain clauses of this contract were adopted, for instance, he stated that the scarcity of labour was the justification for something that had been put into this contract, he uses it. The labour question is used by the right hon. Prime Minister where it suits him to justify some unreasonable clause in this contract, but when the question is raised for the purpose of protecting the labourers of this country, and not allowing the question to be used as a foot-ball to allow a big corporation to break its contract with the government, no attempt is made to explain how it is that the omission referred to by the hon. gentleman who has raised this question was permitted to occur, and no attempt is made to show that the suggestion offered by hon. gentlemen on this side of the House is not for the best. The right hon. Prime Minister has also had pointed out to t iin that there is no comparison between the ability of the Grand Trunk Pacific to construct this road and the ability of the Canadian Pacific Railway to construct their road.
L myself desire to say that I know not much about the western country except what I have learned by hearing hon. members of this House describing it, but I can well understand that there can be no comparison as to the ability of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company to construct their line more quickly than the Canadian Pacific Railway were enabled to construct their line, which was built twenty-odd years ago. TV hy is that ? The Canadian Pacific Railway not only have a large trunk line through that country, but we know that they have almost innumerable branch lines running across the country, which are able to carry everything that is required for the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific to within perhaps a few miles of any point on the prairie section of the new road. Now, what is the effect of that ? The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company can be building their line in twenty different places on the prairie. They can have twenty construction gangs working at the same time. They Can build ten miles at a stretch and couple them together in a day or two. The Canadian Pacific Railway bad to make their own trail and stick to it. There was no railway at that time on which to carry anything required for the construction, except their own railway as it was built, and they were obliged to build only in one place at a time, gradually crawling forward and increasing the mileage of their line, 'on which they carried all the materials necessary for the construction. But the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company to-

day have the benefit of the Canadian Pacific Railway main line and of all their branch lines to carry everything necessary for the construction of the road, and they can construct it in ten, fifteen or twenty-mile sections. Therefore, there is every reason why the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company should be bound to build at once on tha prairie section, instead of making the construction of that section contemporaneous with the building of the mountain section. At the risk of being called names and of making the right hon. Prime Minister angry, we have to ask ourselves why this matter was not attended to. We have to explain to the people of this country why it has not been attended to. If we do not get an answer from the right hon. Prime Minister when we ask for information, we are justified in inferring that there was some reason which the right hon. gentleman does not desire to give. As we cannot find out by a direct question what the people ought to know, in the absence of that answer we are justified in assuming that this arrangement was due to the incompetency or indifference of the government. I do not know what the reason may be, but I am inclined to think that it was due to their carelessness or their disregard of the people's rights, the right hon. Prime Minister not troubling himself as to whether he was making a good bargain or not, but simply desiring to have a railway constructed so that he may be in a position to bring on the elections. The voters who go to the polls in the elections will vote to suit themselves. They want to know what is the best to do for themselves. They want a railway constructed into the Northwest Territories, but they want it constructed in a reasonable way. They want a contract made with some reasonable idea of protecting their interests in the ordinary way, in the same way that they themselves will think of doing. When the request was made to have this clause amended so that the time would be extended, the right hon. Prime Minister no doubt said : I will not say that I will divide it into two sections for the purpose of construction, although I will divide it into two sections for the purpose of paying the money upon it, because of the fact that I may be accused of pettifogging and quibbling if I do so. When this request was made to him, he might have been expected to have said : When you ask for this extension on both sections, what are you prepared to give for it 1 What is the consideration you will give in return for our allowing you three years more time to build the prairie and mountain sections together, and to give you, to that extent, a better contract than you have at the present time with the people of the Dominion ? One would have thought that he would have considered the question in that light. I do not know whether he did so or not. I would like to know if the right hon. gentleman would be kind enough to tell us whether he did so or not ? If he will not, we cannot help our-Mr. LANCASTER.
selves. I would have thought that he would have said : Seeing that you want so many advantages and that you want three years more to construct this railway, particularly the prairie section, we have to fight a general election some time within three years or less, and I think, Mr. Hays, that you should allow me an opportunity of going to the people and finding out whether they want this contract or not. You should give me three years to do that, instead of asking me to give you three years' extra time in which to construct this railway. If the right hon. gentleman assumes that he is going to be premier always, and that the people cannot do anything to prevent him from being premier, we can understand why he did not think he ought to ask Mr. Hays to give him an opportunity of ascertaining whether the people wanted this contract or not; but this we can assume, that the people really do own Canada, and that the voters are really the people who have the right to say whether they shall have this contract or not. Now that the right hon. gentleman's attention has been drawn to the matter, it may not be too late yet, because this contract has not been ratified. It is subject to the ratification of parliament. I would suggest that the right hon. gentleman should send a cablegram, or write a letter, to the Grand Trunk Railway people explaining the circumstances under which he is placed, stating that the hon. gentlemen of the opposition have been asking questions which he is unable to answer, and asking for further time in which to consider this contract.
Why should not the government beseech the Grand Trunk Railway to help them out of the difficulty ; why should they not go to the Grand Trunk and say : we are not able to answer a question about even the first clause of the contract, give us a couple ' of years to reconstruct our cabinet, and find a Minister of Railways who will defend the contract, and then we can appeal to the people and find whether they want this contract or not. After all, it is not the Prime Minister who has to pay the shot; it is the taxpayers of this good Dominion of Canada who will have to put up the money to meet all the responsibilities assumed by us under this contract. I hope that the Prime Minister will not call me the hard names he called the member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker), but even at that risk I would point out to him with all due deference, that seeing that the Grand Trunk Railway Company has discarded last year's contract, the people of Canada, the other partners to the contract. should have an opportunity of saying whether they will endorse it or not. Under all these circumstances, we should have some more light thrown on this contract by the ministers.

The hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) made a very strong statement when he declared, that there was a tacit understanding between the Grand

Trunk Railway Company and the government with respect to the surveys east ot Winnipeg. There was a question asked in the House some days ago about this matter, and I say that the answer given by the government is not in accord with the statement now made by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Barker). If the Grand Trunk Railway are making surveys east of Winnipeg, probably with a view of building their branch lines to Port Arthur and North Bay, these surveys will be made for their own purpose of getting the most convenient route from the transcontinental railway to these two points. Why should the government pay for these surveys ? This is a very important feature of this whole transaction. If the line is to be built from Winnipeg tb Quebec and Moncton, the government should see to it that the Grand Trunk surveys for their branch lines should in no way be such, as might effect the grades or curvatures on the main line. It is the duty of the Prime Minister to reply to that statement of the hon. member for Hamilton.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have no objection to answer the statement at the proper time, but I would ask my hon. friend, if this question has any relevancy to the clause under discussion ?

I believe it has great relevancy and great concern for the people of Canada. It is a simple question, and it can be easily answered if the right hon. gentleman wants to expedite business. If the government does intend to pay the Grand Trunk Railway for surveys they are making the right lion, gentleman can say ' yes.' and if not, he can say ' no.'

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I cannot say ' yes ' or ' no.' I do not know if the surveys will prove to be useful and if they are useful I suppose there would be no reason why they should not be paid for, but if they turn out to be absolutely useless, I do not see yvhy we should pay for them. I may say that at the present time there is no understanding whatever with regard to these surveys.

We should have from the government a plain statement of what they propose to do, and what they do not propose to do. Like the Prime Minister, I wish to be a little modest about my business ability, but it does occur to me that the businesslike way would be for the government to take charge of the surveys from Winnipeg to Moncton. The Minister of Justice told us to-night that all railway companies were selfish, and that being so their selfishness would lead them to make the surveys in their own interests, and not in the interests of the people of Canada. We should guard against that. I may not be very long in parliament, and other gentlemen may not be long in parliament, but I
am immodest enough to predict, that if the government ever does build this line from Winnipeg to Moncton, so far as the operation. of it goes, the Grand Trunk Railway will be more exercised about getting the freight from Winnipeg to Port Arthur or North Bay, than in bringing it east to Quebec.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I trust that gentlemen will confine the discussion to the question before the chair, which is, the propriety of extending the time for the construction of the western division. '
I am sorry you have not given this matter the consideration you ought to give it, as chairman of the Committee of the Whole, allow me to say that we are now considering this whole agreement.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The question is on clause 1 : the extension of time.
My understanding is that we are considering the first section of the Bill.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: No ; the first clause of the schedule.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: If I* understand it aright, my hon. friend from Hamilton did discuss the first section fairly, and the right hon. the Prime Minister wandered away from it and called him a pettifogger anil used other words not at all applicable to the first section ; and yet the chairman did not call him to order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: During the discussion of these matters there are frequently little flurries between members, and when these pass over, the members get back to the question. But when a distinct question is brought up, of course I must rule upon it.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: That is quite right ; but my hon. friend from Hamilton did not say a word that did not apply to the first clause ; and yet the Prime Minister got up and abused him and the chairman did not call him to order. What is sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander.
What I said, Mr. Chairman, did not meet with your approval.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is under a mistake. It was agreed at the beginning, instead of taking up the clauses of the agreement, to take up the schedule ; and the first clause of that was read, and the discussion was supposed to be upon that.
Was that agreement in writing ?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It was between the members across the floor.
I understood that after the other night all agreements were to be in writing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That was between the whips. There is no need of agreements made between members across the floor being in [DOT] writing. We have ' Hansard ' to put them on record.

The Prime Minister, by the personal remarks which he addressed to the hon. member for Hamilton, is not likely to facilitate the passage of this Bill through Parliament. He rather invited discussion by the manner in which he addressed members on this side of the House, and if we wished to retaliate in kind, we might say that as representatives of the people who are here to perform their legitimate duties, we do not object to being lectured by the Prime Minister, but we certainly object to being bulldozed, and we propose to discuss this question even though our opinions may differ somewhat from those of the Prime Minister ; but because of that difference I do not think we deserve to be characterized as pettifoggers or quib-blers. The Prime Minister has said that it would be an onerous condition to impose on the Grand Trunk Pacific Company that they must construct the 1,000 miies of the prairie section in a shorter time than the whole of the western extension. But, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Pope) before six o'clock, Mr. Hays, when getting his charter through the Railway Committee, was quite willing to promise almost anything in order to get it through. When asked by some members if the company would commence construction on the Moncton section simultaneously with the Quebec to Winnipeg section, he answered in the affirmative. It will be no more onerous to have that stipulation imposed with reference to that portion of the line which is going to be the easiest to construct and the most profitable, namely, the portion between Edmonton apd Winnipeg. Therefore I think the Prime Minister was not offering a very good reason for not imposing on the company the stipulation for the completion of that section in five years. I do not think we should accept the mere word of the Grand Trunk Company that they are going to construct that line before the expiration of the eight years, when they are not bound to do so in black and white. We know exactly how much dependence we may place on the word of mouth of any corporation, and the Grand Trunk Company are probably no better or^ worse in this respect than any other. We have already had experience of the manner in which this corporation keeps its written contracts with parliament; and the Northwest members display a degree of gullibility and innocence not excelled by Mark Twain's * Innocent Abroad.' in being willing to extend the time of construction to eight years, on the pretense that they Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
know the company will complete it long before the expiration of that time. If they think the company is going to complete it before the eight years expire, this is the time to say so in black and white. The company have already caused an infraction of their agreement in the matter of making the deposit. The government used just such arguments last session in regard to that matter; and yet we found that before thirty days elapsed, the company refused to put up their deposit in cash or government securities. They did this, not because they could not raise the money, for Mr. Hays said they could get plenty of it, but they resorted to the bonds of the Grand Trunk Railway Company simply as a matter of convenience to themselves. If they so treat their written contract with parliament, why should we be asked to take their word of mouth that this road will be completed long before the expiration of the eight years ? I think it is unreasonable for them to expect that, in view of our experience with them in regard to the deposit. The Prime Minister states that the prairie section of the railway will go through a country where it will be very remunerative from the first day of its operation. I agree with him if we know where it is to be located ; but at present we do not know. It may go through that part of the country between the Canadian Northern and the Canadian Pacific, which is already pretty thickly settled ; and if so, it would be imposing no onerous condition upon the company to require them to construct the line in five years, as was provided in the contract adopted last session. We cannot tell what contingency may arise to cause the company, in their business interest, to refuse to implement their contract in this particular ; and in a few years we may find them doing what they are doing this year-coming back to parliament and asking for an extension of time even beyond the eight years. Therefore, as a western man I refuse to agree to extend the time for three years, for that portion of the road which is to be constructed through a country that is badly in need of railway accommodation, and where the railway is going to be very profitable to operate. Now, the objection that has been taken to the scheme of the hon. leader of the opposition by some hon. members from the west is because it means delay. Why do they say that it means delay ? Simply because the leader of the opposition proposed that he should take the best expert opinion he could possibly secure as to where the road should be built, as to the character of the road and all matters pertaining to the construction of a profitable line, viewed from the country's standpoint. This could have been done in a few months, but simply because the leader of the opposition wanted that matter referred to a commission of

experts, we had these hou. gentlemen from the west making the objection that that meant delay. Yet now we find them supporting the proposition of their own leader for greater delay, by extending the time limit of construction from December, 1908, to December, 1911, and I have not the slightest doubt that if the right hon. gentleman had asked an extension of time for fifteen years, we would have found these same gentlemen giving him their solid support. They are bound so closely by their party interests that they wou 1<1 certainly sacrifice the interests of their constituents rather than refuse to acquiesce in the decision of their leader. And if the government desired to cut down the limit from five years to three, they would equally herald that as the very acme of statesmanship. No matter what the government may propose, it will always receive the enthusiastic support of these gentlemen. But, however much they may be counted upon to support any government measure, it is quite evident that the cloture has been applied to them in this matter. It is quite clear that the policy of silence has been deemed most fitting to the situation in which they find themselves, and (that they think it more prudent not to commit themselves by any remarks in this House, not to bind themselves down to any utterances that may appear in 'Hansard,' and thus avoid having to answer for their words to their own constituents.
" hen the discussion was up last year, the same argument which these hon. gentlemen used with regard to delay in construction, they used with regard to the question of rates. A motion was presented from this side providing that this company should not impose any higher rates to the head of the great lakes than would be charged by the Canadian Northern Railway, but these gentlemen voted down that resolution and gave as a reason for their action their full conviction that even cheaper rates would be charged by the Grand Trunk Pacific than would be exacted by the Northern Railway, The hon. member for West Assiniboia went so far as to state that if he thought the contention of the opposition was correct, if he thought the Grand Trunk Pacific would charge higher rates than the Canadian Northern, unless this amendment were passed, he would support it, but such was his confidence that the Grand Trunk Pacific would charge - lower rates, that he felt bound to record his vote against it. How very gullible are these hon. gentlemen. What innocent trust they display in the good faith of this corporation, which has already broken faith with the people of Canada, is exemplified to-day in their willingness to extend the time limit to eight years for the building of this prairie section. They are willing to extend that time limit because they are convinced that the company will 72
build the road in less time. Well, I have not the same childish faith in this or any corporation which is not bound down hard and fast by statute.
We had the question of the location of the road discussed briefly this afternoon. I have here a map circulated by authority of the Department of the Interior, which shows the proposed location of the Grand Trunk Pacific. Hon. gentlemen will notice the very wide extent of country which the red line on this map covers. It scales 100 miles to the inch and covers a strip of territory 25 miles broad, so that the people are being deceived to the extent of 12 or 13 miles on each side, and every farmer is being persuaded that he will have the road running right along side his farm. We have heard from the right hon. the Prime Minister this afternoon that no plans, specifications or profiles have so far been submitted to the government for approval, yet here is a map authorized by the Department of the Interior, circulated in the county of Marquette-because the line runs through that county-and we have the Winnipeg ' Free Press,' the inspired organ of the Minister of the Interior, trying to persuade the people that the member for Marquette is opposing the construction of another line through his constituency, and possibly of one if not two branch lines, which may be constructed as feeders to the main line. How is it that the Minister of the Interior and the organ which supports him have so much knowledge when the government know practically nothing? The surveys *which the Grand Trunk Pacific have been carrying on have not yet been submitted to the government, they do not know .where the line is going to run, yet here is a map sent out by the Department of the Interior for the purpose of deceiving a section of the people of the west into the belief that then1 locality is to be served by the construction of that line. It is to this we take exception. We take exception to this map being made use of by the Liberal candidates in Marquette and Dauphin. The Liberal candidate in Dauphin, not only carries his map around, but goes to tlie extent of saying that if the Grand Trunk Pacific line is not constructed north of the Canadian Northern Railway, through his constituency, he will not be the government candidate. Well, Sir, the line cannot serve all the districts these gentlemen are trying to persuade the people it will, and when we ask the government to tell us where the line is going to be located, surely we are only making a reasonable request. Surely, after all these months during which the surveyors of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway have been out, the government should have more definite information regarding the location of the road, and be able at least to inform us whether it is going to run north or south of the Canadian Northern Railway.



We have had to-night a certificate of character given by the Prime .Minister to himself. We have had him tell us in the past that he was a free trader, but he is so ho longer. He has also been a protectionist, but neither is he that now. He is simply a practical man. He admitted to-night that he is not a business man. I do not think we require to be told that, because this contract carries that impress on it in almost every line. This contract is the result of negotiations between the right hon. gentleman and Mr. Hays, one of the best business men in the railway world to-day, and it certainly gives the conviction that the general manager of the Grand Trunk Railway is a business man. The Prime Minister is quite correct in his estimate of himself when he lays no claim to being a business man, but fancy this important contract, involving an expenditure of some $150,000,000, a large portion of which will have to be paid in cash, being negotiated all through on the part of Canada by a gentleman who is not a business man. For weeks and months the right hon. gentleman was closeted in negotiations with one of the best railway managers on the continent, and did not even call to his assistance the only business man in his cabinet, so far as railway matters are concerned, I refer to Mr. Blair, a gentleman who could have given my right hon. friend valuable advice, which, if followed, would have resulted in a saving to the country of many millions of dollars. However, Mr. Blah' stepped out from the right hon. gentleman's cabinet, and would no doubt be to-day an active opponent of the present scheme had he not been shelved with the splendid emolument of $10,000 per year for the next ten years. But there is another gentleman who ought to be the business man on railway matters of the present cabinet, the hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson.) Where is he? We rarely see him in this House. I think it is a most humiliating position for any gentleman to occupy, who signed this contract on behalf of the people, that he should not be even in the House to defend a single clause of that contract. No explanation has been offered by the Prime Minister or his colleagues why the Minister of Railways is not here to defend the policy of tne government and the contract to which he himself attached his own signature. But probably the hon. gentleman, having put himself on record last session in ' Hansard,' as being in favour of government ownership of railways, finds the time too short in which to swallow himself. After having last session advocated the extension of the Intercolonial Railway to the shores of Georgian Bay, he probably finds it difficult to explain why he to-day takes the very opposite position and condemns the leader of the opposition for proposing that very scheme. Realizing his embarrassing position, the hon.

gentleman no doubt regards discretion as the better part of valour and prefers to remain entrenched behind the lines of Torres Vedras.
The hon. members for Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee) and Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) discussed at some length the question who are employed on those surveys. I do not know how much credence to place on that circular sent out by the Canadian engineers; but inasmuch as it has been brought up on several occasions and has never been contradicted by members of the government, I take it that the information it gives is accurate. And, when we are talking about this road opening new avenues of employment for our young men and so keeping them within our own borders rather than allowing them to go to a foreign country, I think we have a right to ask how it comes that Canadian engineers, perfectly competent for this work and desiring employment, are passed over and aliens are given the preference. I do not wonder that the company are asking for an extension of time for three years wheu they are employing alien engineers. I am informed that these engineers are the laughing stock of that western country. They are floundering about in an effort to get a suitable location. But they do not know that country.
I am glad to see that the Minister of Railways (Mr. Emmerson) has come in, and that he looks so smiling. I have no doubt that, when I ask him for his opinion as to the extension of the Intercolonial to Georgian Bay, he will be only too glad to rise, after I have taken my seat, to explain his position and defend his speech of last year.
I was explaining that the alien engineers employed by this Grand Trunk Pacific Company seem to be making but slow progress. I do not wonder that their progress has been so slow, and that, so far, they have had no specifications to lay before this government. Not knowing the geography of the country, not understanding the surveys they have been largely following the old Fleming survey, as I am informed. They have not been able to make the progress with the surveys of the road that would have been made if Canadian engineers had been employed on the work. For my part as a western member, I think the question that has been brought up with regard to the construction of the prairie section is most important ; and I for one, express dissent when I am asked, in the face of the experience we have had with this company, to take the word of mouth of members of the company as sufficient assurance that they will finish the prairie section within five years. If the government think that their statement that the prairie section will be rapidly built is sufficient, and if they think it will be in the interest of the company to build the prairie section within five years, it will impose no burden upon them to bind them to finish

within that time. If the government will do this, they will find that, so far as I am concerned,'the section will go through with very little discussion.

Since the Minister of Railways has come in, I am sure he will be a good listener while I explain to him the arguments that have been put forth. In the absence of the hon. gentleman certain re a-sons have been given whyi there should be no extension of time for the construction of the prairie section. It is said that there is a scarcity of men to engage in railway construction, and that this may delay the work. The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals comes from the province of New Brunswick, where population has been stagnant for ten years because there has been a steady exodus of its people to foreign countries. Surely the hon. gentleman will interest himself in bringing sufficient men from that province of New Brunswick to the Northwest to engage in the work of railway construction. It must be remembered that, though the Minister of Railways and Canals is a man of few words, he is a man of great resource. Let me remind the House of an incident of last session which showed the hon. gentleman to be a master of unlimited resource Complaint was made that, throughout the whole Dominion, there was a great deal of American silver in circulation which, by reason of age and use, had become worn and deteriorated. In the absence of other silver, Canadians were forced to receive this depreciated American currency in the course of trade, but, when they took it to the banks they found that it would not be accepted at its face value. This question staggered even the Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding)-he was speechless, powerless, paralyzed. Nor was the First Minister able to come to his rescue. Then arose that man of genius the Minister of Railways and Canals and gave a solution of the problem in the twinkling of an eye. True, he was not then Minister of Railways, but only a quiet and unobstrusive member of the House. He was not then bowed down with weight of woe-as he appears to have been since-and with the responsibilities of office. But, when this problem of the American silver was brought before the House, his gigantic brain power, his massive intellect, his wonderful fertility of resource, enabled him to point the way out. i He said : Pass a law to make the banks take American silver at par. And what do you think happened then ? Why, when the hon. gentleman sat down smothered with the applause that greeted his magnificent idea, somebody pointed out to him that banks were only collections of men and women holding stock in these concerns, and that to compel them to take a depreciated dollar and give a gold dollar for it would be to take money out of their pockets.
I am going to appeal to that hon. gentleman, translated as he has been to a higher
72}
sphere of usefulness. I hope nobody said * uselessness.' I say 1 usefulness.' There are times when one can appear very wise by keeping quiet. I do not mean to insinuate that the Minister of Railways has a monopoly of that. Because I am willing to concede that, if, throughout this whole discussion he has looked wise, he has been outvied by the ministers from Ontario who have looked even wiser and have been as completely silent as the hon. gentleman himself. I intend to direct my argument to him. It has been argued, and argued very strongly, that there will be difficulties in the way of railway construction within the next few years and so it will be fair to allow these railway projectors a further time of three years in which to finish the road. Does the Minister of Railways and Canals think that is right ? Remember that this whole scheme is in the interest of the people of the Northwest. In part of the country through which this projected railway is to run, we have already a tide of immigration setting in. The Minister of Railways and Canals knows that, at a point west of Battleford, there is what is known as the large Barr colony. The country attracted those colonists there. The colonists went in last fall ; they are plowing this spring and it is to be hoped they will be reaping magnificent crops this harvest. How are they going to get their grain out ? I know perfectly well that the Minister of Railways and Canals has all in his mind. If not, I will pass over to him a folder of the Canadian Pacific Railway that 1 have here, which explains all the circumstances. What an outcry there would be if these people are unable to get out their grain. They will say : Here we were attracted by assurances of a railway communication at an early day, and the parliament of Canada has done nothing to compel this company to live up to this understanding, but has granted them a further extension of time. I am appealing now to a practical railway man, because the Minister of Railways and Canals would not have been installed in his present office had not he been a practical man. I am going to ask the minister, with his practical knowledge of engineering and railway matters, if he does not think it possible, with all the modern facilities, to construct a railway over a prairie at the rate of three miles a day. The Minister of Railways acquiesces in that. So, we are at one in that respect.
I know that the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Emmerson) has a most exalted opinion on the Grand Trunk Pacific Company ; in fact its greatness has staggered him into silence. That is the only reason he has not defended it ; he is awed by its very appearance on the horizon. I asked the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Emmerson) what he thinks of this as a proposition. Mr. Mackenzie, president of the Canadian Northern, was

interviewed in Winnipeg yesterday, and be made tbe statement that the Canadian Northern will this year build no less than 600 miles of prairie railway. If this compari-tively small concern, the Canadian Northern, are going to build 600 miles, does he not think that this fondling of his should be able to double or treble that. I am not much of a Shakespearian reader but I remember that in the great play of Julius Ceasar. when an actor appeals to a high magnate, he uses that famous phrase :
I pause for a reply.
Now I pause for a reply from the great Caesar. If the Minister of Railways and Canals will not answer me. I am sure he will disappoint his admirers on this side of the House and we will have to look upon him in the light of the lines in Grey's Elegy as being :
Some mute, inglorious Milton here may rest Some Cromwell guiltless of his country's blood.

I notice that on the supplementary agreement the name of Henry Robert Emmerson, Minister of Railways and Canals is used. Either that hon. gentleman's frank has been used or he has signed this document and if he has signed the document surely he will tell us why he has signed it, and why this change has been brought about as between the government and the Grand Trunk Pacific. If the hon. gentleman refuses to do that, I can only remind him that he must have been reading some of the speeches made in this House last session. Probably he has been reading the speech of the hon. member for Huntingdon, who, speaking cf the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals, because the late minister took the opportunity of explaining his position on this Transcontinental Railway, said :
After the pettiness, smallness and temper which the hon. gentleman showed in the speech he made in this House, I have come to the ' conclusion that he is not as large a man as 1 thought he was.
Probably he has been reading that speech and has concluded not to say a word in connection with this, but to allow the First Minister and the Minister of Justice to handle this Bill in the House. The position which the hon. gentleman occupies is the most humiliating spectacle I ever witnessed. Here is a gentleman occupying this position, who has signed this document making these changes, and yet he cannot say a word in the House as to why he did so. It is essentially a Bill which he should explain. While the Minister of Justice is a good lawyer, this is not his line of business, nor is it the special line of the right hon. the premier. Therefore, the Minister of Railways and Canals is the one to whom we should look for an explanation, but be says nothing. The opposition have treated Mr. BENNETT.
this measure extremely kindly. When hon. gentlemen opposite were in opposition, the rafters of this building would rise with condemnations of the opposition of that day against anything of the kind. We were told that the Minister of Trade and Commerce, was simply a fifth wheel on a wagon, neither useful nor ornamental, and what would they have said if we had a minister who was afraid and declined to state why he signed a public document involving a cost to this country of $170.000.000. I do not wish to use unparliamentary language, but I must say that if the hon. gentleman had the spirit in him which he ought to have, he would rise in liis place and state exactly why he signed the document and whether he justifies it or not. Personally I have the very highest regard for the Minister of Railways, and I believe he is possessed of greater abilitv than his silence now would lead ns to believe.
