That being so, I say it is his duty to rise in his place and give some explanation and I trust before the matter is closed, he will do so. Hon. gentlemen on this side of the House will make the platform of this country ring with this statement, that the government have a Minister of Railways and Canals who has not the courage to get up and explain his signature. Hon. gentlemen opposite will talk about this being a good project and about this being a business government, but we will be able to reply :	imagine a business
government having a Minister of Railways and Canals, who dare not rise in his place and tell the people why he signed a document. Talk about pettifogging, talk about quibbling. My hon. friend was not even quibbling, but I am bound to say it was a good deal like pettifogging. This will do him a great deal of harm. Let me again draw the attention of the First Minister to the fact that there are many men on his side of the House competent to occupy positions in the cabinet. There can be no doubt about that. Here we have an hon. gentleman who held a prominent position in the local government of the province of New Brunswick, who has been but a short time in this House, who, during that short time, made remarkable headway as a private member, and who has now been placed In the important position of Minister of Railways and Canals. Now, Sir, there is one of two things ; either this hon. gentleman was possessed of the ability and experience necessary to induce the right hon. leader of the government to appoint him to that position, or there must be some political reason outside of his ability that caused the right hon. Prime Minister to select him. Unless the right hon. First Minister gives the reason why his Minister of Railways and Canals does not do this, or unless the right hon. gentleman himself explains, the government will be in a very bad fix. The right hon. First Mims-

ter liad a competent Minister of Railways and Canals in his government. There is no man, either on the government side or on this side of the House, who questions the ability of the Hon. Mr. Blair. But the right hon. First Minister did not treat the hon. gentleman as very much of an expert when he entirely ignored Mr. Blair in framing the first agreement. He ignored his Minister of Railways in bringing about that agreement, and now he has either ordered his present Minister of Railways to say nothing, or he is ignoring him in the same despicable way that he ignored the other one. It is a very unhappy position that the government are in, and I will tell the right hon. First Minister that when they go to the country, because we are going to the country before long, this will be one of the strongest things that can be urged against the government. The people of the country, and the farmers especially, will ask if this is the kind of government they have, if this is the govern ment who are paying enormous salaries to ministers of the Crown-because they look . upon the salary of a minister as something extraordinary, more than we as members of this House do-who has failed to open his mouth on a question involving $171,000,000 of the people's money. This is the most humiliating spectacle that I have ever witnessed in this House, and I go further and say that it is the most humiliating spectacle that has ever been known in this world.
The CHAIRMAN {Mr. A. Johnston). Shall this section be adopted ?

You seem to be in a hurry ; there is lots of time. Time was made for slaves, not for members of parliament who have to consider great questions. The right hon. leader of the government (Sir Wilfrid i.aurier), in presenting this Bill, laid great stress upon the prospect of the development of that section of the country to the north of Lake Superior and down to Quebec. He told us about the quality of the timber growing there-jack pine and poplar-and expressed his opinion that in the future a great pulp-wood and lumber business would be developed. The right hon. gentleman did not turn that great practical mind of his to good account in considering that question, because we will remember that the right hon. gentleman has told us that he was a practical man above all other things, that he did not pretend to be a man of great business experience or capacity, that he was not a free trader, that he was not a protectionist, that he had been both and now he was neither, but that he was a practical man. As such he should look upon the question of the settlement of that northern country in a practical way. You cannot remove the timber rapidly from that country through which you are going to build this railway, because if you undertake to clear that country rapidly, you have to go back to the old system of burning up the Umber. There is
no other way that you can bring about rapid colonization or turn that northern country to account as a practical country for settlement unless you go back to the old-fashioned way of fifty years ago and destroy the forest by burning it. The slow process of removing the timber for the market as the demand will require will not permit settlement in that district.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: As a practical man, my hon. friend (Mr. Pope) is not speaking on the question at all.
Certainly, the question is on the first clause.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No ; the first clause of the schedule-the extension of time.

Let me have the first clause. Well, Mr. Chairman, is it true that we have been talking on the wrong clause all this evening ? Is it a fact, Sir, that we have to begin this thing all over again ? I would like to know from you whether I have to take those two speeches back that I have made ? I think it is unkind of the right kon. First Minister, who has now returned to his pleasant mood again, that he should have allowed me to go on with that laboured effort and then tell me that I was not talking on the right clause. We knew on this side of the House that we were not talking on the right kind of a Bill. We knew that last year. The right hon. Prime Minister did not, but he found it out after we prorogued. He has discovered that the whole of the speeches delivered last year on both sides of the House were wasted. I am not so certain. But when I look at this Bill, i wonder who signed it-' Henry Robert Em-merson, Minister of Railways and Canals.' Mr. Chairman, I wonder where he comes from. I would like to know what part. The right hon. gentleman objects to my referring to that northern country and to the forests of jack pine and poplar, and I suppose he will even object to my referring to that rose that bloomed up there 250 years ago. It must be somewhat faded now. In view of the fact that under this amended contract the government have eradicated from the old contract of nine months ago every provision which they said protected the interests of the public ; and in view of the fact that this new contract has been dictated by the officials of the Grand Trunk, and every clause of it drafted to satisfy the most skeptical shareholder of the Grand Trunk, I will leave it to some other hon. member to characterize this document as it deserves.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
In the course of his speech delivered some days ago, the Minister of the Interior regretted that the surveys which had been made were not returned from the Grand Trunk Railway to the government so that they could be * laid before the House; the hon. gentle-

man gave to the House an abstract of these surveys which he said had been procured from the Grand Trunk Railway Company in Montreal by the geographer of his department. I wish to know from the government, what the nature of these surveys was, and especially how it happens that the Grand Trunk Railway is making surveys of the eastern division, which according to the contract, is to be built by the government. It would appear that notwithstanding the haste which the right hon. gentleman emphasized last year, the government has in the interval done nothing with regard to making surveys, and for some reason the Grand Trunk Railway Company have been making surveys from Winnipeg as far east as North Bay. Why is it that the government has not made surveys of the eastern division, and why have they been compelled to resort to the Grand Trunk Railway Company for information as to the practicability and cost of a railway which is to be built by the government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have no objection to answer that question at the proper time, but does my hon. friend think that it is relevant to this question which we are discussing.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I would answer that question, by asking my hon. friend another. If it does not come under this section where does it come? It comes up somewhere, because it was introduced by the Minister of the Interior, otherwise he would have been out of order in bringing it before the House. I am not particular about bringing it up now, if the right hon. gentleman will point out when it can be brought up properly, and answered by the government ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It can come up in many ways ; it can come up on the second reading, and in concurrence on the resolutions, but it is certainly not relevant to the question we are now discussing.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I am entirely at the service of my right hon. friend as to the time and place of discussing this matter, but I submit that the proper time to discuss it is during the committee stage.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It would come up on the first general section which has been suspended, but now we are discussing the question of the extension of time.
Are we not discussing the whole Bill ?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: No ; the schedule.
Then the clerk of the House deceived me by putting this Bill in my hand. I appeal to the Prime Minister for protection.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have no objection to give it to my hon. friend ; either Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
the clerk of the House or my hon. friend have been too green.
I plead guilty but I thought the clerk of the House was not so green.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There was an arrangement made between the leader of the opposition and the Minister of Justice this afternoon as to how they would proceed .and the arrangement was that the first section of the schedule would be taken up.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The chairman has slightly misunderstood any arrangement which was made. The Minister of Justice suggested to me that the best time to take up the schedule was in connection with the section which ratified it, but as to limiting the discussion upon any particular clause, it is news to me that I assented to anything of the kind. I am perfectly willing to enter into any arrangement which would be regarded as convenient, but the view I take is that the schedule is ratified by the section, and that everything is open for discussion when you are considering the schedule. That I understand to be the rule, apart from any arrangement.

I do not insist on discussing the subject now, but I do insist on discussing it at some time.
' Mr. POPE. I am glad to know that I am not the only green one in this House, but that I have a good deal of company. The effort to ripen some people seems to have made them greener than before, and with the permission of the House, X will return this Bill to the Clerk.

I understand that the matter more immediately under discussion at present is the amendment relating to the extension of time ; and the point that seems to be important is the effect it may have on the condition and prospects of the people living in the prairie portion of country through which this railroad is to be extended. The great objection to the extension of time is that it applies to that portion of the road which in the opinion of most people interested in the question is the part which requires immediate consideration and immediate service, that is, provided any one is prepared to admit that the Bill is providing a public work of necessity. I listened to-day with a great deal of interest to the remarks of the hon. Minister of Justice in reference to this matter. As nearly as X could gather, his argument was . that this extension of time was not objectionable, because the interests of the company would lead it to construct that portion of the road in the shortest possible time. To follow his remarks to a logical conclusion, there would be no reason why the company should npt have an unlimited extension of time. If the whole matter were to be decided in that way, then it would be sufficient to make the contract with the company without putting in any restriction whatever, but leaving it entirely in the hands of the company to build the road whenever they saw fit, relying upon their selfish interests to build it promptly. It would be most extraordinary for the parliament of Canada to favour arguments of that sort, because no contracting parties ever make contracts on these terms-the one party being bound and the other being left free. Business arrangements always bind both parties. In illustration of the correctness of his view, the hon. Minister of Justice cited the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, which was bound to build the railway within ten years, and which actually did build it in five years or less than six years; and he argued, if I understood him aright, that if the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, being bound to build their road in ten years, built it in five years, therefore, the Grand
Trunk Pacific Company, being bound to , build their road in eight years, would build it in four years. That may be a perfectly legitimate conclusion, and the result may justify it. At the same time, the question would very naturally arise in the minds of the people of Canada that it is an extraordinary thing that the government, in making such a contract of such a character as this, should not make it in such terms as would express the expectation of the country. The country will naturally ask, if the government expect the road to be built in four years, why should they make a contract to have it built in eight years? But I would remind the hon. Minister of Justice that his memory of that matter is not altogether accurate, because, although the Canadian Pacific Railway Company contracted to build their railway in ten years, and built it in five years, the expectation of the country at the time was that it would take them ten years to build it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Did I make any statement different from that?
There was no reliance on the selfish interest of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to build it in less than ten years. The Minister of Justice made a statement entirely at variance with that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I did not.

I think I can persuade the Minister of Justice himself of that. He said that as the Canadian Pacific Railway Company had built their road in less than half the time in which they contracted to build it, this company might be expected to build their road in half the time in which they contracted to build it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I never made any such statement.

In that case I misunderstood the hon. gentleman, and must modify the argument I inteude(d to make on that point.
The Conservative government, when it made a contract with the Canadian Pacific Railway and gave ten years to construct their road, believed that they would require all those ten years. If the government of that day had thought that the company could have done the work in five years, they would have made that the limit and required the company to complete it within that period. But the general opinion then was that all the ten years would be required. The late Mi'. Alexander Mackenzie, no mean authority on the subject, said all the power of the British empire could not build that road in ten years, the time in which the Canadian Pacific Railway had undertaken to build it. I am therefore safe in arguing that if the government of that day had anticipated that the Canadian Pacific Railway could have built the road in less than ten years, they would have made the time limit

shorter than that period. But here you find the government extending the time to eight years, and then telling us that they do not believe the company will take that long. But the objectionable feature is this, that the limit of eight years is made to apply to the whole undertaking of the company, that consisting of the entire line from Winnipeg to the Pacific coast. We must bear in mind that the government in this contract has carefully distinguished the prairie section from the mountain section. And we find gentlemen interested in the prairie country objecting to this provision as not being in the public interest. The object of building this line was to give immediate relief to the people who are suffering for want of railway accommodation, but by this extension we are enabling the company to occupy eight years in traversing a country through which railway construction is comparatively easy instead of the five years provided in the first contract. What is the reply of the government to the arguments of the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. W. J. Roche) and Macdonald (Mr. Boyd)? They argue simply that the company having put up $5,000,000, they represented to the govern-men that possibly this money might be jeopardized by delaying the construction of the road, and the government, without considering apparently the real conditions of the contract, acceded to that request and agreed to delay the construction of the work on the prairie section. What reason is there why the government should give this extension, ns far as the prairie section is concerned ? There seemed to be every inducement ou the part of the government, not to relax the original conditions, but rather make- them more stringent. We all remember the arguments advanced by the First Minister last year. His principal argument was the danger of the bonding privilege being abrogated. His next argument was the urgent necessity of affording relief to the people suffering from the evils of congested traffic. In the most emphatic way, he endeavoured to convince the House that there was no time for delay, and in fact gave us to understand that if Canada did not provide this railway at once, a great deal of our western traffic would be diverted over United States lines. Yet we find the government to-day acceding to the demand of the company for delay. It is impossible to reconcile the different positions taken by the right hon. gentleman. Either there was not that urgency which last year he said existed, or he has lost every particle of his desire to meet that urgent demand. What does the contract require of the company with regard to the prairie section V It requires that they should build about a thousand miles of railway. Over what kind of country ? Over one of the most suitable countries for rapid railway construction to be found in the world-a prairie country, a Mr. BELL.
country far different now from what it was in the days when the Canadian Pacific Railway was built. Then it was uninhabited and without any railway facilities, whereas to-day it is filled with people and served by railways, so that there will be no difficulty in the Grand Trunk Pacific bringing in both labour and supplies. There can be no doubt that this company will be able to build their line much more rapidly than the Canadian Pacific Railway did theirs. The experience' of the Canadian Pacific Railway is at their service ; the very engineers who did that work for the Canadian Pacific Railway in some measure are available for the use of this company to-day. All the experience, all the errors, all the failures of the Canadian Pacific are spread out for their instruction. The untold advantages of the experience not only of the Canadian Pacific but of the Canadian Northern as well will enable them, if they choose to do it, to make a record-breaking speed of railway construction across that country. What would be a reasonable rate of railway construction there now that labourers, materials and supplies can be deposited easily at different points on the line of construction ? Would it be too much to believe that the company, commencing at various portions of this line and employing various bodies of men, could build at the rate of three miles a day ? Commencing at half a dozen points if they please, they should be able to complete the road at the rate of at least three miles a day. They could have three gangs working at different points, or they could subdivide the work as much as they please, as every portion could be reached. How long, then, should the company require to build this prairie section of 1,000 miles ?
Fifteen years.

Allowing three hundred working days in the year, and three miles a day. we find that 900 miles could be built in one year, and not fifteen years as has been suggested by an hon. gentleman. And yet we find the government allowing eight years to complete the contract; because this is an- extension of time to eight years not for the mountain section or for the prairie section, but for the whole, division. And so, they are allowing eight years for the construction of a work vrhich could be easily, and without extra cost or exceptional effort, finished in one year. That being the case, is it surprising that hon. gentlemen who represent constituencies in Manitoba a r d the Northwest, raise their voices in protest against the proposal to extend the time to eight years ? Is it not natural that they should ask the government that has introduced this measure, and is calling upon the people of Canada to make enormous sacrifices for this road on the ground that it is to be built for the purpose of removing the disabilities now resting upon the people

of the Northwest Territories, why is it that they propose to allow eight years for this work ? The situation really becomes far-cial and ridiculous when you regard it in that aspect. And, when this question is asked, what is the reply vouchsafed by the government ? Practically there is none. We have the Minister of Railways under whose department the work is supposed to be carried on, who is to be advised, we are told by a director who will supervise the work, and will report to the Minister of Railways, and from the Minister of Railways the government will receive information as to the progress of the work. What does the Minister of Railways have to say to the reasonable proposition put forward from this side ? He has been appealed to over and over again to give his opinion on this subject, to explain this anomaly in the contract ; and, on every occasion when he has been in the House and has been appealed to he has replied at once with a broad smile. Apparently the hon. gentleman who is now Minister of Railways has never in his life heard any jocose proposition so entirely to his liking as the idea that he should know anything about railway construction in which the government of Canada is interested and for which the people of Canada are supposed to supply all the money. It appears to be, in the estimation of the Minister of Railways, representing in this respect, the government, and the Prime Minister of Canada- the hugest of jokes that he should be supposed to know anything at all about this enormous and expensive railway contract. If the object is to give the position of Minister of Railways to a gentleman wTlio can wear the honour most gracefully and with the least expenditure of time and trouble, I must say that the position has fallen to a gentleman who lias qualifications that simply cannot be surpassed. But if the cabinet is to be supposed to carry on fairly the business of the country, if it is to be composed of men gathered by the Prime Minister as representative men and possessed of the greatest ability for the discharge of their duties, and the serving of the people, I say that to the people of Canada who regard the spectacle from day to day in this House, there can be nothing reassuring and satisfying. The gentlemen on this side who are asking these questions, who are here to try to learn from the government why certain things are not provided for, will look with surprise and disapproval upon the spectacle of a government that has, apparently, no reasonable answer to give to reasonable questions addressed to them by the opposition, who represent the people. The government do not represent the people in this matter to as large an extent as do the opposition!. The government represents a policy which, so far as we can learn from our observation, is entirely a pet policy developed and carried out by the Prime
Minister, apparently without the support and sanction of his colleagues in this House, because he cannot induce any of these gentlemen to support his policy by speech or even to answer reasonable requests of members on this side. The opposition represent all the people who are not In the confidence of the government-and I need scarcely bay that that seems to be all the people of Canada, outside the sixteen or seventeen gentlemen who constitute the cabinet itself. There are anomalies and peculiarities abojt this contract that are entirely incapable of solution by any one who is not in the secrets of the government, and the government apparently are determined not to unfold these secrets in response to any kind of reasonable request, Now, if it be that this is a policy of the Prime Minister himself, if it is a policy that he is following out of his own volition and by the power he exercises over the people of Canada, the parliament of Canada and the gentlemen he has gathered about him as a government, then, to him would we appeal rather than to anybody else. And what is the result of appealing to him ? He does not give us information ; but he does occasionally give us criticism which we on this side do not consider altogether fair. He denounces arguments which we consider reasonable and fair, as pettifogging, as carping, os simply embarrassing criticisms addressed to bim for the purpose of impeding the course of this Bill through the House, whereas I maintain that the criticisms from this side are reasonable requests of the people of Canada as voiced here by the opposition, as the representatives of the people.
Now, why should the company be given this time ? Why should the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, the Grand Trunk Company-for we have every reason to believe that it is the Grand Trunk-be given this extension of time V Is it because the company cannot raise the money to build this road ?
The right hon. gentleman knows that there are provisions in the contract by which that company can come to his government and compel it to supply them, by an issue of interim bonds, with enough money to build the road. The credit of Canada'is at the back of their scheme and as soon as this contract becomes the law of this country the company will not be hampered for the want of money. If the company were compelled to finance this scheme and raise the money there might be some excuse for having that extension of time and to make allowance for the fact that there might be times when the money market would be unfavourable. But that is not the position of affairs. The government of Canada have to supply the money for the building not only of the eastern, but of the western section of the road. That being the case, it cannot be for want of funds that this

great extension of time is granted. Why then is it? Is it because the right lion, gentleman has made up his mind to furnish to this country an absolute refutation of the statement with which he introduced this Bill a year ago, when he urged the rapid construction of this road? Does the right lion, gentleman wish to proclaim to this country and to the world that when he made these passionate appeals he was playing on the ignorance of his hearers, the supposed ignorance of this country? Now that the scheme is being launched as a fact it will be shown by the course of events that there is not one atom or tittle of sincerity in any one word which the hon. gentleman uttered in urging the necessity for the rapid building of the road. There can be no Justification for the spirit in which the right hon. gentleman introduced the Bill. If there is. urgency for relief in the west the government could easily induce the company to undertake the completion of the western prairie section, not in eight years, but in two years, because the Grand Trunk Pacific is able to make use of the whole credit of the Dominion of Canada for the building of its road from Winnipeg to Edmonton. Nothing could be more reasonable than the criticism of this clause of the Bill. We all know that great national interests are involved in having this railway built into the prairie country as rapidly as possible. If there is any part of this country on which it would pay Canada to spend money freely it would be in that prairie country, because as any one can see, every dollar spent on improving the means of communication in the west must quickly bring in golden returns to the treasury and promote the general prosperity of the country. Why then will the right hon. gentleman not abate one feature of this contract, objectionable to the people of the west, or vouchsafe a reasonable explanation of this part of the contract or allow one member of his cabinet to give such an explanation? The western section is divided by the government into two sections, and why should the government insist on applying this extension of three years to the whole western section instead of limiting it to the part of the road which lies between the foothills on the eastern edge of the Rocky mountains and the Pacific coast. If any part of this work is to be proceeded with hastily it unquestionably is' the part from Winnipeg west, and yet this may be delayed for eight years. This is simply a case of a party holding power with a large majority dictating a certain course to an opposition, and refusing absolutely to vouchsafe any explanation in reference to it. I need scarcely say that the whole project as outlined to this House and to the Committees of this House last year is important not only to the provinces or territories of the west, but to the whole of Canada.
But I do clearly remember that to the young men of Canada, to the people of Can-Mr. BELL.
ada generally, this scheme was unfolded as a great scheme, as a scheme requiring the strength of a powerful government, as a scheme intended to aggrandize the people of Canada, to give us a new Canada, to relieve the hardships and burdens of the pioneers of the west, and to promote the welfare and prosperity of the manufacturing interests in the east by binding this country more closely together by an iron bond. That was represented to us as being a matter of the greatest possible urgency. We were told that we were in such a position that the greatest possible amount of the wealth that we might develop by our industry in this country was liable to be at any moment diverted from us by our enterprising neigh hours to the south for all time to come ; and yet we find the government in reference to the easiest possible part of their scheme, that part of the scheme which unquestionably can be constructed with a less amount of cost and difficulty than some other parts of the scheme, binding themselves to a period of eight years within which that work is to have its completion. To the people of the east this is a great object lesson. If it is a fact, in the opinion of the right hon. First Minister and of his advisers and supporters, that the prairie section cannot be built hi less than eight years, I would like to ask the right hon. gentleman in what time he thinks he can construct the road from Quebec to Winnipeg and from Quebec to Moncton, and at what period of time he is going to hold out hopes to his supporters in the cities of Halifax and St. John that the great tide of commerce is going to reach those cities. It will not be within the reign of the right hon. gentleman who is now premier of Canada. It will be at a time so far removed that the events of to-day will have grown as hazy to the people of that day as the events of the time of the conception of the Canadian Pacific Railway seem to us to-day. The fact is that the government have undertaken to legislate, not for the people of this generation, but for the people of the next generation. It is not statesmanship, it is not practical politics. It goes to show that when the right hon. gentleman introduced this measure into the House last session he had no clear conception of what the government were undertaking, but he had in his own mind a fiction, a figment, a dream, and in the representation of that dream he hoped to bewilder the mass of the people of the country so as to bring to himself for the time being a specious kind of glory, a specious advantage that might perhaps enable him to snatch an uncertain success at the polls. What does it all amount to when you come down to examine it ? Nothing more than that. The right hon. gentleman apparently was trying to place himself upon a level with that great man, that honourable and great statesman who really gave us a transcontinental railway-the late Rt. Hon. Sir John Macdonald. Before passing off the stage he

wished to immortalize himself as the projector and constructor of another transcon tinental railway. He wished to build himself a monument which would span the whole continent, resting upon the Atlantic and the Pacific, so that he would go down in history and in the memory of the people who are going to follow us as a companion figure to that great man Sir John Macdonald who did give to this country a great constructive work which has made Canada a nation-the Canadian Pacific Railway. With the assistance of his majority in this House and a very reasonable amount of criticism from this side of the House, every portion of which was intended to better his scheme, to free it from its objections, to make it more valuable to this country, the scheme passed through the House and if it resulted in failure it was not the fault of hon. gentlemen on this side of the House. There is no reason why the right hon. gentleman should lose his temper with hon. gentlemen on this side of the House because his progeny proved a frail bantling incapable of successful life or growth. But, why should the right hon. gentleman have taken the trouble in the amendments which he has introduced into this scheme to demonstrate not only to the members of this House but to the people of the country as well, to the commonest observer, to the simplest man who can say that two and two make four, that every word that he said last year was tainted with insincerity and betokened an ignorance of the conditions that attach to a well considered and practicable scheme.
Now, it is very possible ~ that the right hon. gentleman could put any kind- of a scheme through this parliament and could do it by sheer force of numbers, by the sheer weight of votes, that without the utterance of one word or one argument he could force any measure he chose through this House, but if he should succeed in doing that he must fail in obtaining the support from the country that; ought to be given to a government that can give a reason for the faith that is in it. In all the discussion that has taken place in reference to this great measure-because it is a great measure when you regard it in reference to its extent, although it is a measure which is perhaps greater in its breach than in its observance- I have not heard addressed to this House from this side.one single argument against that measure which seemed to be based on anything but sound reason tendered to the House in the spirit of honest and earnest criticism intended to improve that measure for the benefit of the country. How has that conduct on this side of the House been met by hon. gentlemen opposite ? It has not excited in their breasts a great deal of admiration. They must have learned from their experience in this House to admire patriotic, generous sentiments even though they see them in their opponents. But, it places them in a most extraordinary position
because we find a collection of hon. gentlemen-reverend seigneurs, some of them possibly the representatives of the best brains of the Liberal party, sitting absolutely dumb and silent utterly unable to furnish answer, argument, demurrer or reply of any kind whatever to the most reasonable proposition that could be addressed to them in attack of the measure that they have brought before the House. An extraordinary spectacle such as this almost looks as if that system of machine government, beginning in the province of Ontario in the election of their representatives, is now to be found in the halls of parliament as well and that the whole system of government has become one huge voiceless machine. There is great pressure in the weight of numbers. A measure is introduced and forced through parliament. There is no illuminating intellectual explanation to us why it should go through. There is no intelligence in its progress. It is simply, apparently, a return to the time when force was the only argument in the world that was of any value. Here you have a cabinet which we were told in 1897 and later was the greatest cabinet that had ever been assembled-a collection of choice spirits representative not only of the intellectual ability and power of the Liberal party as reported in the Dominion parliament, but of the Lib'eral party as represented in the parliaments of the provinces as well. Facilis descensus averni. In the course of their eight years of power they are apparently converted into a collection of inarticulate counters in the hands of the master player who pushes them here and there on the checker board as he pleases. It is not our part to quarrel with this amazing spectacle, if the right hon. gentleman chooses to play this game and his followers allow him to continue at it. If something supernatural had given to the opposition in this House the power, to hold up the government of Canada as a spectacle of actual imbecility, the opposition could not have succeeded better, in exhibiting to the people of Canada the spectacle which we now behold, of a government which was lauded eight years ago as the greatest and strongest that had ever been, fall into such a condition of palsied uselessness. It is not in our hearts to find fault, but still, as Canadians we must regret what is occurring in this House at this moment. Is it possible that parliamentary government in Canada is such, that reasonable argument can be addressed by the hour, and by the day, and by the yard, to the government

Mr. BELL-and by the half yard, in order to suit the gentleman from Cape Breton ; I have no objection to giving him a smaller measure. Is it possible that this parliament is reduced to this: that the government will deliberately sit there helpless and silent

and voiceless, absolutely unable to devise one reasonable answer to the reasonable arguments that are addressed from this side of the House? If the right hon. gentleman and his followers choose to adopt that role of voiceless, absolutely responseless conduct, then I should think that the common-sense of the people of Canada will at a very early day restore them to a position in which they can develop their capacity for holding their tongues to a much higher degree than they can here. It is not the part of tlie opposition in this House to furnish brains to the government, but the government should realize that when they choose to muzzle the Minister of Railways, who is properly charged with the conduct of this measure, the people will come to the conclusion that there must be some most extraordinary reason to account for such an extraordinary state of affairs. I ask the Prime Minister why it is that he cannot furnish to the representatives of Marquette and Macdonald, some reason why they can go back to their constituencies and explain to them this proposition to delay the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific for three years? We as an opposition are doing our duty, but how is the government doing its duty? Apparently the government has made up its mind to give no answer at all to the legitimate requests from this side of the House for reasonable information, and that being the case, it seems to me that the wonder is that the opposition'has been able to display such great patience in criticising this measure.

If I could do anything to bring this discussion to a close, I would make the strongest effort I ever did in my life, because we have been here talking on this measure for three weeks, and we are just about where we started so far as converting the government and their supporters is concerned. I have spoken three times before on this question, and I have used all my energy to try and convert the Prime Minister and his followei-s to the ideas of government ownership over this transcontinental line. I have not talked privately to them of course, and I have not used any undue influence, but so far as my voice would go, I have endeavoured to get them to build and own this railroad, for I believe that we must have another railroad in that section of the country, and that right away. 1 thought when the government appointed a new Minister of Railways, that they would go in for government ownership, because if they are going to hand all the railroads of the country over to private corporations, what do they want with a Minister of Railways. We have a commission appointed to look after the railways of this country, and although that commission will cost |30,000 a year, I have no objection to it so long as the commissioners do their duty, but I do not think that there was any neces-Mr. BELL.
sity to tack on to the end of it a Minister of Railways. Mr. R, L. BORDEN. Touched by the appeal of my hon. friend from West Elgin (Mr. Robinson), perhaps we might give him an instalment by letting this clause pass ; but before doing so, I would like to ask my hon. friend the Minister of Justice as to the introduction of the word ' strikes ' in this section. It does not seem to be referred to in the correspondence. Would my hon. friend be good enough to say what is the occasion of it ?	'

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not know that it is referred to in the correspondence ; but our attention was drawn to the possibility of strikes occurring in connection with the enterprise, and my hon. friend will remember that at the present time it is very usual to find in contracts of this description the word ' strikes,' in consequence of the frequency of labour difficulties.
Section 1 of the schedule agreed to.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
As we have done a very good day's work and have passed one clause, I move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.
Progress reported.
On motion of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, House adjourned at 12.05 a.m., Friday.

Friday, April 29, 1904.
